title: Moses as trustworthy witness to creation
english: A fitting beginning for one who is about to speak of the constitution of the world is to set before his discourse the beginning of the ordering of visible things. For the making of heaven and earth is about to be handed down to us—not brought together by chance, as some have imagined, but receiving its cause from God. What hearing is worthy of the greatness of what is said? How ought a soul to come prepared for the hearing of such things? It should be pure from the passions of the flesh, unclouded by worldly cares, diligent, searching, looking around from every side to see if it might gain a worthy thought of God. But before we examine the precision in the words and search out how great are the meanings of these small utterances, let us consider who it is who speaks with us. For even if we cannot reach the deep heart of the writer because of the weakness of our understanding, yet if we attend to the trustworthiness of the speaker, we shall be led of our own accord to assent to what is said. Moses, then, is the one who laid down this writing—that Moses who was testified to be pleasing to God while still an infant; whom the daughter of Pharaoh adopted and raised in royal fashion, appointing the wise men of the Egyptians as teachers for his education. He hated the bulk of tyranny and ran back to the lowliness of his own people, choosing to suffer hardship with the people of God rather than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin (Hebrews 11:25). He possessed friendship with righteousness from nature itself, since even before the rule of the people was entrusted to him, he is seen defending against the wicked even to the point of death because of his natural hatred of evil. He was driven into exile by those he had benefited, and gladly left behind the disturbances of Egypt and came to Ethiopia, and there, keeping himself entirely free from other pursuits, he spent forty whole years in the contemplation of realities. When he was already eighty years old, he saw God as far as it is possible for a human being to see—or rather, as it was granted to no one else, according to the very testimony of God: “If there is a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in sleep. Not so with my servant Moses; he is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in visible form, and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:6-8). This man, then, who was counted worthy of the face-to-face vision of God equally with the angels, speaks to us from what he heard from God. Let us listen, then, to words of truth spoken not in persuasive words of human wisdom but in teachings of the Spirit, whose end is not the praise of the hearers but the salvation of those who are taught.

“In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The wonder of the thought stops my speech. What shall I say first? Where shall I begin the explanation? Shall I refute the vanity of those outside, or shall I praise our truth? The wise men of the Greeks wrote much about nature, and not one doctrine among them has stood fixed and unshaken, since each one always overthrows the one before him. So there is no need for us to refute their teachings, for they are sufficient for one another's overthrow.
orientation: Basil opens his first homily on the Six Days by introducing Moses as the divinely attested author whose account of creation demands a prepared and attentive soul.

title: The world's beginning refutes godless cosmologies
english: Those who did not know God would not allow that an intelligent cause stood over the origin of all things, but drew their conclusions in a way consistent with their initial ignorance. For this reason some fled to material principles, assigning the cause of everything to the elements of the world; others imagined that atoms and partless bodies, masses and pores, hold together the nature of visible things. Now, they said, when the partless bodies come together with one another, and now when they are rearranged, births and destructions come about; and in the case of the more enduring bodies, the stronger interweaving of the atoms provides the cause of their permanence. Truly those who write these things weave a spider's web, setting up such fine and insubstantial principles for heaven and earth and sea. For they did not know how to say, “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). Because of this they were deceived by the godlessness dwelling within them into thinking that all things are unsteered and ungoverned, carried along as chance would have it. So that we might not suffer this, the one who wrote the account of the world's creation at once, in his very first words, illuminated our minds with the name of God, saying, “In the beginning God made.” How beautiful is the order! He placed “beginning” first, so that no one would think the world is without beginning. Then he added “made,” so that it might be shown that what was made is the smallest part of the Creator's power. For just as a potter, having shaped countless vessels by the same art, has not used up either his art or his power, so also the Creator of this universe does not have a creative power measured to one world alone, but one that surpasses it to an infinite degree, and by the inclination of his will alone he brought the magnitudes of visible things into being. If then the world has a beginning and has been made, ask who gave it its beginning and who is its maker. Or rather, so that you may not be led astray from the truth by searching with human reasonings, he anticipated you with his teaching, placing in our souls as a seal and a safeguard the precious name of God, saying, “In the beginning God made.” The blessed nature, the ungrudging goodness, the one beloved by all who have received reason, the much-longed-for beauty, the beginning of all beings, the source of life, the intelligible light, the unapproachable wisdom—this one “made the heaven and the earth in the beginning” (Genesis 1:1). Do not imagine, then, O man, that visible things are without beginning; and do not suppose, because the things that move in the heavens run round in a circle and the beginning of a circle is not easily grasped by our ordinary perception, that the nature of the bodies that move in circles is without beginning. For this circle—I mean the plane figure enclosed by a single line—even though it escapes our perception, and we cannot discover where it began or where it ended, we are not therefore obliged to suppose that it is without beginning. But even if it escapes perception, in truth it certainly began from some point, drawn by one who marked it out with a center and a radius. So you too, because the things that move in a circle return upon themselves, do not let the smoothness of their motion, uninterrupted by anything in the middle, leave in you the error that the world is without beginning and without end.
orientation: Basil is expounding Genesis 1:1, arguing against Greek philosophers who denied that an intelligent cause stands over the origin of all things.

title: The world's beginning implies its end
english: “For the form of this world passes away” (1 Corinthians 7:31), and “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35). These are advance announcements of the teachings about the consummation and about the transformation of the world, delivered now in brief as part of the elementary teaching of the inspired Scripture. “In the beginning God made.” Whatever begins from time must of necessity also be completed in time. If it has a beginning in time, do not doubt about its end. For geometry and arithmetic methods, and the treatises about solid bodies, and the much-talked-about astronomy, the much-busied vanity—to what end do they lead? If those who have devoted themselves to these things have conceived that this visible world is co-eternal with God the Creator of all things, bringing what is circumscribed and has a material body to the same glory as the incomprehensible and invisible nature, not even being able to conceive this much: that what has parts subject to corruption and alteration must of necessity one day undergo the same sufferings as its own parts. But they became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened, and claiming to be wise, they became fools (Romans 1:21-22), so much so that some declared that heaven exists together with God from eternity, while others declared that it is itself God, without beginning and without end, and the cause of the particular ordering of things. Surely their abundance of worldly wisdom will one day bring them an increase of their harsh condemnation, because seeing so sharply into vain things, they were willingly blinded to the understanding of the truth. But those who measure the distances of the stars, and catalogue the ever-visible ones and those near the Bear, and all that lie around the southern pole—visible to some, but unknown to us—and who divide the northern latitude and the zodiacal circle into countless intervals, and who observe with precision the risings of stars, their stations, their declinations, and the forward motion of all of them, and how much time each of the wandering stars takes to complete its own circuit—they have not discovered one single device among all these for conceiving of God as the maker of the universe and a just judge who brings to each the worthy recompense for the life he has lived. Nor have they been able, by the teaching about judgment, to recognize the thought of the consummation that follows from it: that the world must of necessity be transformed, if the condition of souls is also to change to another kind of life. For just as the present life has a nature akin to this world, so also the future existence of our souls will receive an end suited to its condition. But they are so far from attending to these truths that they pour out loud laughter at us when we proclaim the consummation of this world and the regeneration of the age. Since the beginning is by nature set before the things that come from it, when he spoke about the things that have their being from time, he necessarily set this word before all others, saying, “In the beginning God made.” For there was something, it seems, even before this world, which is contemplable by our mind but was left unrecorded, because it was unsuitable for those still being introduced and still infants in knowledge. There was a condition older than the birth of the world, befitting the supercosmic powers, the one above time, the eternal, the everlasting.
orientation: Basil is arguing against those who think the visible world is eternal, showing that because it began in time it must also end, and that the philosophers' wisdom only increased their condemnation.

title: The invisible creation and the meanings of 'beginning'
english: In that world the Creator and Maker of all things brought his works to completion: an intelligible light suited to the blessedness of those who love the Lord, the rational and invisible natures, and the whole ordering of the intelligible realm, all that surpasses our understanding, whose very names we cannot discover. These things fill up the substance of the invisible world, as Paul teaches us when he says, “For in him all things were created, whether visible or invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities or powers, whether angelic hosts or archangelic ministries” (Colossians 1:16). But when it was time for this world also to be introduced among the things that exist, it was first of all a school and training place of human souls, and then also a dwelling place suited to all things in generation and corruption. The course of time, then, came into being as something natural to the world and to the animals and plants within it, always pressing forward and flowing past, never pausing in its race. Is time not exactly this: the past has vanished, the future is not yet here, and the present slips away from our perception before it can be known? The nature of things that come to be is like this too: always either growing or wasting away, with no evident fixedness or stability. It was fitting, therefore, that the bodies of animals and plants, bound as if by necessity to some stream and held fast by the movement that leads them toward generation or corruption, should be contained by the nature of time, which possesses a property akin to the things that change. For this reason the one who wisely teaches us the origin of the world fittingly began his account of it by saying, “In the beginning God made”—that is, in this beginning according to time. For he does not say it came to be in the beginning, testifying that it precedes all created things in age; rather, after the invisible and intelligible realities, he recounts the beginning of the existence of these visible things that are grasped by the senses. “Beginning” is also used of first movement, as in, “The beginning of a good way is to do what is right” (Proverbs 16:5 LXX). For it is from righteous actions that we are first moved toward the blessed life. “Beginning” is also used of that from which something comes, as the foundation is in a house and the keel in a ship, according to what is said: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Proverbs 1:7; cf. Psalm 111:10 LXX). For reverence is like a base and a pedestal for perfection. The beginning of works of craft is the craft itself, as the wisdom of Bezalel was the beginning of the adornment of the tabernacle. And the beginning of actions is often the useful end of what comes to be, as the acceptance from God is the beginning of almsgiving, and the end stored up in the promises is the beginning of every activity according to virtue. Since “beginning” is used in so many ways, consider whether the present word does not fit all its meanings. You can learn from what time the constitution of this world began, if you go back from the present into the past and earnestly seek to find the first day of the world's origin. For in this way you will discover whence time received its first movement, and then that heaven and earth were laid down beforehand like foundations and bases, and then that there is some craftsmanlike reason that guided the ordering of the visible things, as the word “beginning” indicates to you. And you will discover that the world was not devised at random or in vain, but for some useful end and to contribute great benefit to the things that exist, if indeed it is truly a school for rational souls and a training place for the knowledge of God, providing guidance by the hand to the mind through visible and perceptible things toward the contemplation of the invisible, as the apostle says: “His invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made since the creation of the world, are clearly seen” (Romans 1:20).
orientation: Basil is explaining what existed before the visible world and why Genesis says 'In the beginning God made,' distinguishing the invisible creation from the temporal beginning of the visible world.

title: The beginning is not a part of time, and 'made' shows God as craftsman
english: Or perhaps the words “In the beginning God made” were chosen because the act of creation was instantaneous and outside time, since a beginning is something without parts and without extension. Just as the beginning of a road is not yet a road, and the beginning of a house is not a house, so the beginning of time is not yet time—not even the smallest part of it. And if someone argues contentiously that the beginning is time, let him understand that he will be dividing it into the parts of time: beginning, middle, and end. But to imagine a beginning of a beginning is utterly laughable. The person who cuts the beginning in two will make two beginnings instead of one—or rather many, even infinite, since whatever is divided is always cut into further pieces. So to teach us that the world came into existence together with the will of God, outside time, Scripture says, “In the beginning God made.” Other translators, expressing the meaning more clearly, have said, “In summary God made”—that is, all at once and concisely. Let this much suffice, then, as a brief account drawn from many possible remarks about the beginning.

Now among the arts, some are called productive, others practical, and others theoretical. The end of the theoretical arts is the activity of the mind. The end of the practical arts is the movement of the body itself, and when that movement stops, nothing remains or persists for those who see it; for dancing and flute-playing have no end product, but the activity itself terminates in itself. In the productive arts, however, even when the activity has ceased, the work remains before us—as with house-building, carpentry, metalworking, weaving, and all such crafts. Even if the craftsman is not present, these works sufficiently display the skill of their makers in themselves, and you can admire the builder from his building, the metalworker and the weaver from their work. So to show that the world is a technical construction, set before all for contemplation, so that through it the wisdom of its Maker might be known, the wise Moses used no other word about it. He said, “In the beginning God made”—not “he worked,” nor “he brought into existence,” but “He made.” And since many people have imagined that the world coexisted with God from eternity and was not made by him, but rather came into existence automatically as a kind of shadow of his power—they acknowledge God as its cause, but as a cause without deliberate choice, like a body causing its shadow or a light causing its radiance—the prophet corrects this error by using the precise wording, “In the beginning God made.” God did not merely supply the cause of its being; as good, he made what is useful; as wise, what is most beautiful; as powerful, what is greatest. He has all but shown you a craftsman entering into the substance of all things, fitting each individual part to the others, and producing a whole that is consistent with itself, harmonious, and perfectly ordered. “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.” By the two extremes of the universe he indicated its existence obliquely, giving the heaven the first place in origin and saying that the earth holds second place in existence.
orientation: Basil is expounding the first words of Genesis, 'In the beginning God made,' and has just begun his first homily on the six days of creation.

title: The extremes imply the middle; do not probe the substance of heaven or earth
english: And certainly whatever lies between these two also came into being together with the extremes. So even if Moses says nothing about the elements—fire, water, and air—you should understand by your own reasoning, first, that all things are mixed with all things. In earth you will find water, air, and fire: fire leaps out from stones, and from iron—which itself has its origin from the earth—abundant fire is wont to flash forth in friction. This is worth marveling at: fire exists within bodies and lurks there without harm, but once it is called outside, it is destructive of those guarding it for a time. Well-diggers show that the nature of water is present in the earth, and the vapors rising from earth moistened and warmed by the sun show the presence of air. Then further, if heaven by nature occupies the upper region and the earth is the lowest—because light things are carried toward heaven, while heavy things naturally sink down toward the earth, and up and down are most opposite to each other—then the one who mentioned the things most distant from each other by nature also indicated by synecdoche the things that fill the space between them. So do not seek an explanation of each individual thing, but understand what was passed over in silence through what was spoken.

“In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.” The investigation of the substance of each existing thing—whether of those that fall under our contemplation or of those set before our senses—would introduce a long and detached discourse into the exposition, so that more words would be consumed in examining this problem than all the rest that can be said about each of the questions. And this would be of no benefit for the building up of the Church. But concerning the substance of heaven, we are satisfied with what Isaiah said. In simple words he gave us an adequate understanding of its nature when he said, “He who made firm the heaven as smoke” (Isaiah 40:22)—that is, he gave the heaven a fine nature for its composition, not a solid nor thick one. And concerning its shape, what he said is sufficient for us, when he said in praise of God, “He who set the heaven as a vault” (Isaiah 40:22). Let us give ourselves the same counsel concerning the earth: not to busy ourselves overmuch with its substance, whatever it may be, nor to wear ourselves out with reasonings by seeking out the underlying reality itself, nor to seek some nature devoid of qualities, existing without quality by its own definition. Rather, we should know well that everything observed about the earth is ordered toward the principle of its being, and these things complete its substance. For you will arrive at nothing if you try by reasoning to strip away each of the qualities that exist in it. If you remove the black, the cold, the heavy, the dense, the qualities of taste that exist in it, or any others that are observed about it, there will be no underlying reality left. So I urge you to leave these questions aside, and not to seek on what the earth stands. For the mind will grow dizzy this way too, as the reasoning proceeds toward no agreed-upon end.
orientation: Basil is expounding Genesis 1:1, arguing that by naming heaven and earth Moses indicated all that lies between them, and he now warns against inquiring into the substance of heaven and earth.

title: The earth's support and the philosophers' theory of its central place
english: For if you say that air is spread beneath the breadth of the earth, you will be at a loss how a soft and porous nature endures being squeezed by such a weight, but does not slip away on every side, fleeing the settling down and always pouring upward past whatever compresses it. Again, if you suppose for yourself that water is what lies beneath the earth, you will likewise ask how the heavy and dense does not sink through the water, but is held by a weaker nature though it so greatly exceeds it in weight. And then you will seek the seat of the water itself, and again be at a loss about what watertight and resisting base its lowest bottom rests upon.

And if you suppose that some other body heavier than the earth prevents the earth from moving downward, you will reflect that that body too needs something similar to cover it and keep it from falling. And if we can contrive something to place beneath that one, our mind will seek again the support of that one, and so we will fall into infinity, always devising other bases for the bases we keep finding. And the further we advance in reasoning, the greater the counter-resisting power we are forced to introduce, one that can push back against the whole weight above it at once.

For this reason, set a boundary to your thought, lest the word of Job overtake you for your meddling as you peer into things incomprehensible, and you too be asked by him, “On what are its rings fastened?” (Job 38:6). But if you ever hear in the Psalms, “I have made firm its pillars” (Psalm 74:3 (LXX)), consider the power that holds it together to be called pillars. For what does “He founded it upon the seas” (Psalm 23:2 (LXX)) indicate, except that the nature of water is poured around the earth on every side? How then, since water is flowing and naturally falls downward, does it remain suspended and never flow away? But do you not consider that the earth hanging by itself, being heavier in nature, presents the same or even greater difficulty for reasoning?

But it is necessary, whether we grant that the earth exists by itself or say that it rests upon the water, never to depart from devout thinking, but to confess that all things are held together by the power of the Creator. So we must say to ourselves, and to those who ask us on what this immense and unbearable weight of the earth is supported, that “In the hand of God are the ends of the earth” (Psalm 94:4 (LXX)). This is safest for our understanding and beneficial for our hearers.

Already some of the natural philosophers cleverly devise such causes for the earth remaining unmoved. They say that because it has taken the middle place of the universe, and because of its equal distance on every side from the extremity, it has nowhere to which it might incline more, and so necessarily remains upon itself, since the surrounding likeness on every side makes any inclination in any direction entirely impossible for it. And they say the earth did not obtain the middle place by lot, nor by chance, but that this position is natural and necessary for the earth. For since the heavenly body occupies the outermost place as regards the upward direction, he says, whatever weights we suppose fall from above will be brought together from every side to the middle.
orientation: Basil is addressing the question of what supports the earth, arguing that every proposed support leads to an infinite regress, and that the only safe answer is that God's power holds all things together.

title: The earth's natural place and the philosophers' theories of heaven
english: And clearly, wherever the parts are carried, the whole will be pushed together toward that same place. If stones and wood and all earthy things are carried downward, then this would also be the proper and fitting position for the whole earth. And if any light thing is carried from the middle, clearly it will move toward the highest point. So the proper movement for the heaviest things is downward, and reason has shown that downward means toward the middle. Do not be surprised, then, that the earth never falls out of place, since it holds the middle as its natural position. For it is absolutely necessary that it remain in place, or else, if it moves contrary to nature, it departs from its proper seat. If any of these arguments seems persuasive to you, transfer your wonder to the wisdom of God who arranged things this way. For amazement at the greatest things is not diminished when the manner in which something marvelous happens is discovered. But if not, then at least let the simplicity of faith be stronger than logical demonstrations.

We might say the same things about heaven as well: the wise men of the world have composed very many-worded treatises about the heavenly nature. Some have said that it is composed of the four elements, since it is tangible and visible, sharing in earth because of its resistance, in fire because it is seen, and in the remaining elements because of the mixture. Others, rejecting this argument as unconvincing, introduced a certain fifth nature of body for the constitution of heaven, improvising it from themselves and by themselves. And among them there is something called the ethereal body, which they say is neither fire nor air nor earth nor water, nor in general any one of the simple bodies. They reason that the simple bodies have movement in a straight line as their proper motion, light things being carried upward and heavy things downward. But upward and downward are not the same as circular whirling, and in general a straight line differs enormously from revolution in a circle. And things whose natural movements are different must necessarily, they say, also have different essences. But neither can we suppose that heaven is composed of the primary bodies, which we call elements, because things composed of different materials cannot have smooth and unforced movement, since each of the simple bodies present in composite things has one impulse or another from nature. Therefore composite things are first of all held together with labor in their continuous movement, because one movement cannot be well-fitted and congenial to all the opposing elements; rather, the movement proper to the light element is hostile to the heaviest. For when we move upward, we are weighed down by the earthy element; and when we are carried downward, we do violence to the fiery element, dragging it down contrary to nature. And this dragging of the elements in opposite directions is an occasion of falling apart. For what is forced and contrary to nature, after resisting for a little while—and that violently and with difficulty—quickly dissolves into the things from which it was composed, as each of the elements that came together returns to its proper place.
orientation: Basil is answering objections about why the earth stays in place, then turns to what the wise of the world have said about the nature of heaven.

title: Against the fifth element and the call to glorify the Creator
english: Because of these constraints of reasoning, as they say, those who rejected the arguments of their predecessors needed a hypothesis of their own—the ones who posited a fifth nature of body for the generation of the heaven and the stars in it. Then another of those who swell with plausible argument rose up against them in turn, and he scattered and dissolved their views, introducing his own opinion instead. If we now tried to speak about these matters, we would fall into the same endless chatter as they do. But let us leave them to be overthrown by each other, and let us set aside the question of substance. Persuaded by Moses that God made the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1), let us glorify the master craftsman of all that has been made wisely and skillfully, and from the beauty of the visible things let us contemplate the one beyond beauty, and from the magnitude of these perceptible and circumscribed bodies let us reason by analogy to the one who is infinite, beyond all magnitude, and who surpasses every mind in the abundance of his power. For even if we do not know the nature of the things that were made, still what falls wholly under our perception holds so much wonder that even the most skilled mind proves inferior to the least of the things in the world—inferior either to the task of expounding it worthily, or to the task of rendering the praise owed to the Creator. To him be all glory, honor, and might, forever and ever. Amen.
Homily 2: On the earth being invisible and unformed

This morning we lingered over a few small words, and we found the depth of their meaning so hidden that we utterly despaired of what follows. For if the outer courts of the holy places are like this, and the gateways of the temple are so majestic and overwhelming, dazzling the eyes of our mind with the excess of their beauty, what must the holy of holies be? Who is fit to dare enter the inner sanctuaries? Who can look upon the secret things? Their very sight is unapproachable, and the word that would explain what is understood is altogether hard to utter. Nevertheless, since with the righteous judge there are appointed rewards not to be despised even for the mere choice of what is right, let us not shrink from the search. For even if we fall short of what is worthy, if we do not miss the intention of Scripture with the help of the Spirit, we too will not be judged altogether worthless, and with the cooperation of grace we will provide some building up for the Church of God.

Now the earth was, it says, invisible and unformed (Genesis 1:2). How is it that when heaven and earth were both made at the same time, the heaven was completed, while the earth is still incomplete and unworked? Or what, in any case, is the unformed state of the earth? And for what reason was it invisible? The complete formation of the earth is its abundance: the sprouting of all kinds of plants, the putting forth of the tallest trees, both fruitful and unfruitful, the bright colors and sweet fragrances of flowers, and all the things that a little later were about to spring up at the command of God and adorn the earth that gave them birth. Since none of these yet existed, the text rightly called it unformed. We could say the same things about the heaven as well: it too was not yet finished, nor had it received its proper adornment, since it was not yet illuminated by moon or sun, nor crowned with the choirs of the stars.
orientation: Basil is concluding his refutation of pagan theories about the heavens and turning to the proper response: glorifying God from the visible creation.

title: Why the earth is called invisible; against those who posit uncreated matter
english: For none of these things had yet come to be. So you will not stray from the truth if you say that the heaven too was unformed. Scripture calls the earth invisible for two reasons: either because there was not yet a human being to see it, or because it lay submerged beneath the water spreading over its surface and could not be seen. The waters had not yet been gathered into their own gatherings, which God later gathered together and named seas. What then is invisible? One kind is what is not by nature able to be seen by the eyes of flesh, like our mind. Another kind is what is visible by nature but is hidden because a body covering it stands in the way, like iron in the deep. In this latter sense we understand the earth to be called invisible now, since it was covered by the water. And further, since light had not yet come to be, it was no wonder that Scripture also called the earth invisible for this reason: it lay in darkness, because the air above it was unlit.

But the counterfeiters of the truth—those who do not train their own minds to follow Scripture, but twist the meaning of the Scriptures toward their own wish—say that matter is indicated by these words. For this, they say, is by nature both invisible and unformed: without quality in its own right, separated from every form and shape. The craftsman, they say, took it in hand, shaped it by his own wisdom, brought it into order, and so through it gave being to the visible world. Now if this matter is unbegotten, then first of all it is equal in honor to God, deemed worthy of the same privileges. What could be more impious than this—that the qualityless, the formless, the uttermost formlessness, the unformed ugliness (I am using their own terms) should be deemed worthy of the same preeminence as the wise and powerful and all-beautiful craftsman and creator of all things? And further, if matter is so great as to receive the whole knowledge of God, then in some way they set its substance alongside the unsearchable power of God—if indeed it is sufficient to measure out through itself the whole understanding of God. But if matter is less than God's activity, then their argument turns into an even more absurd blasphemy: they would have God held back from his own works, ineffective and inactive, for lack of matter.

But the poverty of human nature has deceived them. Among us, every craft is occupied with some particular matter—metalworking with iron, carpentry with wood—and in these things one thing is the underlying material, another the form, and another the finished product that results from the form. The matter is taken from outside, the form is applied by the craft, and the finished product is what is composed from both, from the form and the matter. So they suppose it is also with the divine creation: the shape of the world was brought in by the wisdom of the maker of all things, but the matter was supplied from outside to the creator, and the world came to be composite—having its underlying substance and being from elsewhere, but receiving its shape and form from God.
orientation: Basil is explaining the phrase 'invisible and unformed' from Genesis 1:2, and now turns to refute interpreters who claim it refers to eternal, uncreated matter.

title: God creates matter itself, not just form
english: From this they go on to deny that the great God presided over the constitution of all things, and to claim that he was like a contributor to some common feast, throwing in only a small portion of his own toward the origin of things. They could not, because of the lowliness of their reasoning, look up to the height of the truth: that here among us the crafts come after their materials, since they were introduced into human life by the necessity of need. The wool existed first, and weaving came afterward, supplying from itself what nature lacked. The wood was there, and carpentry took it in hand, shaping the material for whatever need was sought at the time, and showed us the usefulness of wood—providing an oar for sailors, a winnowing fork for farmers, a spear for soldiers. But God, before any of the things now seen came to be, set his mind to it and resolved to bring the things that were not into being; at one and the same moment he thought what kind of world it should be, and generated together with its form the matter that suited it. For heaven he set apart the nature proper to heaven; for the shape of the earth he supplied the substance that belonged to it and was owed to it. Fire and water and air he shaped as he willed, and brought them into being as the principle of each thing that came to be required. And the whole world, being of unlike parts, he bound together by some unbreakable bond of friendship into one communion and harmony, so that even the things most distant from one another in position seem to be united through their mutual sympathy. Let them cease, then, from their mythical fabrications, measuring by the weakness of their own reasoning the power that is incomprehensible to thought and utterly inexpressible by human speech. “God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1)—not each halfway, but the whole heaven and the whole earth, the very substance taken together with the form. For he is not a discoverer of shapes, but the maker of the very nature of things. Otherwise let them answer us: how did the active power of God and the passive nature of matter ever meet one another—the one supplying the underlying thing without form, the other possessing the knowledge of shapes without the matter—so that each might receive from the other what it lacked: the maker having somewhere to display his craft, and the matter putting off its formlessness and its lack of shape? But enough on these matters. Let us return to the beginning. “The earth was invisible and unformed” (Genesis 1:2). When Moses said, “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), he passed over many things in silence: water, air, fire, and the qualities that arise from them. All of these, as things that complete the world, clearly came into being together with the whole; but the account left them out, training our mind toward quickness, giving us from a few starting points the ability to reason out what remains. Since, then, nothing is said about the water—that God made it—but it is said that the earth was invisible, consider for yourself by what covering it was hidden from view. Fire could not have covered it, for fire gives light and makes visible whatever it comes near, rather than casting darkness.
orientation: Basil is refuting the philosophical idea that matter existed before God and that God only shaped it, arguing instead that God made both the form and the substance of all things.

title: Water and darkness explained literally, against heretical myths
english: Nor was air the covering of the earth at that time. The nature of air is thin and transparent: it receives every form of visible things and passes them on to the eyes of those who see. What remains, then, is for us to understand that water lay spread over the surface of the earth, since the moist substance had not yet been separated off to its own proper place. And for this reason the earth was not only invisible but also unformed. For even now an excess of moisture hinders the earth from bearing fruit. The same cause, then, accounts both for its not being seen and for its being unformed—if indeed the furnishing of the earth is the order proper to it and according to nature: grain fields swelling in the hollows, meadows green and bursting with varied flowers, fertile glens, and mountain peaks shaded by forests. None of these it yet possessed. It was in labor with the birth of all things through the power placed in it by the Creator, but it was waiting for the appointed times, so that at the divine command it might bring forth its offspring into the open.

But “darkness,” it says, “was over the deep” (Genesis 1:2). Here again are other starting points for myths and beginnings of more impious fabrications, for those who twist the words to their own private notions. They do not explain darkness as it actually is—air without light, or a place shadowed by the blocking of a body, or in general a place deprived of light for whatever reason—but they explain darkness as an evil power, or rather evil itself, having its origin from itself, opposed and contrary to the goodness of God. For if God is light, they say, then clearly the power arrayed against him would be darkness, according to the logic of their thought. Darkness, they say, that does not have its being from another, but is a self-begotten evil. Darkness, an enemy of souls, a maker of death, the opposite of virtue. And they are deceived into thinking that this darkness both exists and was not made by God, on the basis of the very words of the prophet. From this, what wicked and godless doctrines have not been fabricated? What heavy wolves, tearing apart the flock of God, have not taken their start from this little phrase and spread over souls? Were not the Marcionites from here? Were not the Valentinians from here? Was not the abominable heresy of the Manichaeans from here—which one would not be wrong to call a gangrene of the churches? Why do you run so far from the truth, O man, devising for yourself starting points of destruction? The word is simple and easy for all to grasp. The earth was invisible, it says. What is the cause? Because it had the deep spread over it. And what is the meaning of “the deep”? Much water, hard to reach, whose limit is downward. But we know that many bodies often appear through water that is thinner and clear. How then was no part of the earth shown through the waters? Because the air poured over it was still without light and darkened. A ray of the sun passing through waters often shows the pebbles in the depths; but in deep night no one could in any way see what is under the water. So the statement that follows confirms that the earth was invisible: because the deep was what covered it, and this deep was darkened. Therefore the deep is not a multitude of opposing powers, as some have imagined; nor is darkness an original and evil power arrayed against the good.
orientation: Basil is explaining why Genesis says the earth was invisible and unformed, arguing that water covered it and the air above was dark, and he begins refuting those who make darkness an evil power.

title: The nature and origin of evil
english: For two things equal to each other in opposition will be entirely destructive of each other's constitution; and they will have and provide unceasing trouble, forever locked in war with one another. And if one of the opposing forces surpasses the other in power, it becomes entirely consuming of the one overcome. So if they say the opposition of evil to good is equally balanced, they introduce unending war and perpetual destruction, with each side conquering and being conquered in turn. But if the good surpasses in power, what is the reason that the nature of evil has not been completely destroyed? And if evil is unbegotten—which is not lawful to say—I wonder how they do not flee from themselves, submitting themselves to such unlawful blasphemies.

Nor is it pious to say that evil has its origin from God, because none of the opposites comes from its opposite. For life does not give birth to death, nor is darkness the source of light, nor is sickness the maker of health. In changes of conditions, the shifts are from opposites to opposites; but in origins, each thing that comes to be proceeds not from opposites but from things of the same kind. If then, someone says, evil is neither unbegotten nor made by God, where does it get its nature? For no one who shares in life will deny that evils exist. What then do we say? That evil is not a living and ensouled substance, but a disposition in the soul opposed to virtue, coming to be in the careless through the falling away from the good.

Do not then look for evil outside yourself; do not imagine some original nature of wickedness. Let each person recognize himself as the originator of his own vice. For of the things that happen to us, some come from nature, such as old age and weaknesses; some from chance, such as irrational misfortunes that befall us from outside causes, often gloomy or sometimes brighter—like the man digging a well finding treasure, or the man hurrying to the marketplace meeting a rabid dog. But some things are in our power, such as mastering desires or not restraining pleasures; such as holding back anger or laying hands on the one who provoked us; telling the truth or lying; being gentle and moderate in character, or puffed up and exalted by arrogance. Of these things, then, of which you yourself are master, do not seek their origins elsewhere, but recognize that evil properly so called has taken its beginning from deliberate falls. For if it were involuntary and not in our power, such great fear from the laws would not hang over wrongdoers, nor would the punishments of the courts be so inexorable, measuring out to criminals what they deserve.

Let this be said by me about evil properly so called. For sickness and poverty and dishonor and death, and all the sorrows of human life, are not yet worthy to be counted in the class of evils, because their opposites are not numbered among our greatest goods. Some of these come from nature, and some appear to have befallen many people for their benefit. So now, silencing every figurative and allegorical explanation for the present, let us receive the meaning of darkness simply and without over-elaboration, following the intention of Scripture.
orientation: Basil is refuting the idea that darkness is an independent evil power, and now explains what evil actually is and where it comes from.

title: Darkness as shadow, not substance
english: But the argument presses further: was darkness created along with the world? Is it older than light? And why is the worse thing the more ancient? And why is the worse thing the more ancient? We answer that this darkness did not subsist in its own right as a substance. It is an affection around the air, coming upon it by deprivation of light. What light, then, did the region within the world suddenly find itself without, so that darkness came to be over the water? We reason as follows: if anything existed before the constitution of this perceptible and perishable world, it was clearly in light. For neither the ranks of the angels, nor all the heavenly armies, nor any named or unnamed rational nature or ministering spirit whatsoever, lived in darkness. They held their proper state in light and all spiritual gladness. No one will dispute this—at least no one who awaits the light above the heavens in the promises of good things, about which Solomon says, “Light is always for the righteous” (Proverbs 13:9), and the apostle says, “Giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified us to share in the inheritance of the saints in light” (Colossians 1:12). For if those who are condemned are sent into the outer darkness, then clearly those who have done what is worthy of acceptance have their rest in the light beyond the world.

So when the heaven came into being by God’s command, suddenly stretched around, enclosing the things within by its own circumference—a continuous body able to separate what is inside from what is outside—it necessarily made the space left within it lightless, cutting off the brightness from outside. For three things must come together for a shadow: the light, the body, and the unlit place. The darkness within the world, then, came to subsist by the shadow of the heavenly body. Understand what I am saying from a clear example: at a still midday, someone sets up a tent around himself made of dense, watertight material and shuts himself inside in a makeshift darkness. Suppose that the darkness in question was like that—not subsisting in its own right beforehand, but following upon other things.

This darkness is also said to walk upon the deep, because the outermost part of the air naturally touches the surfaces of bodies. At that time water lay over everything. Therefore it is necessarily said that darkness was over the deep.

“And the Spirit of God,” it says, “was borne upon the water” (Genesis 1:2). If this means the spirit as the pouring of the air, then accept that the writer is enumerating for you the parts of the world: God made heaven, earth, water, air—and this air already being poured out and flowing. But if—what is more true and was approved by those before us—the Spirit of God means the Holy Spirit, then accept this reading, because Scripture especially and uniquely honors the Spirit with this mention, and nothing else is called the Spirit of God except the Holy Spirit, the completing element of the divine and blessed Trinity. If you accept this meaning, you will find the benefit from it greater.

How, then, was this Spirit borne upon the water? I will tell you not my own word, but that of a Syrian man who was as far from worldly wisdom as he was near to the knowledge of true things. He said that the Syriac language is more expressive, and because of its closeness to Hebrew it somehow approaches the meaning of the Scriptures more nearly.
orientation: Basil is answering the question of whether darkness existed before light and what darkness is, continuing his literal reading of Genesis 1:2.

title: The Spirit's life-giving work and the creation of light
english: So the meaning of the phrase is this. They explain “was borne upon,” he says, as meaning that the Spirit warmed the nature of the waters and gave it life, in the image of a brooding bird that imparts a vital power to the things being warmed beneath it. They say that this word indicates something like this: the Spirit was borne upon the water—that is, the Spirit was preparing the nature of the water for the production of life. From this the question raised by some is sufficiently answered: the Holy Spirit is not absent even from the creative activity.

And God said, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3). The first voice of God created the nature of light, made the darkness vanish, dissolved the gloom, made the world bright, and brought to all things at once a lovely and pleasing appearance. For the heaven appeared, which until then had been hidden by darkness, and its beauty was as great as eyes still testify even now. The air shone round about—or rather, the air held the light wholly mixed through its entire being, sending the sharp transmissions of its radiance everywhere to its own limits. Above, it reached as far as the upper air and heaven itself; in breadth, it illuminated all the parts of the world—north, south, east, and west—in a sharp moment of time. For such is its nature, fine and transparent, that light passing through it needs no extension of time. Just as it carries our sight to visible things without time, so it receives the impulses of light in an instant—in a moment of time smaller than anyone could conceive—to all the limits of the air. And the upper air became more pleasant with the light, and the waters more radiant, not only receiving the radiance but also sending it back from themselves by the reflection of the light, with sparklings flashing from the water on every side. The divine voice transformed all things to the sweetest and most precious state. Just as those who pour oil into the deep make the place transparent, so the Maker of all things, when he spoke, poured the grace of light into the world all at once. “Let there be light.” And the command was a deed; and a nature came into being than which human reasoning cannot conceive anything more delightful for enjoyment.

But when we speak of voice and word and command in relation to God, we do not mean a sound emitted by vocal organs, nor air shaped by the tongue; we understand the divine Word, but we consider the inclination in the will, because it is easily grasped by learners, to be shaped in the form of a command.

And God saw the light, that it was good (Genesis 1:4). What praise worthy of the light could we offer, when it received in advance the testimony of its Creator, that it is good? Among us, too, speech yields the judgment to the eyes, having nothing to say as great as what the senses testify in advance. But if beauty in a body has its being from the symmetry of its parts to one another and from the good color that appears on it, how is the principle of beauty preserved in the case of light, which is simple in nature and of uniform parts? Is it not because what is proportionate in light is testified not in its own parts, but in its painless and gentle effect on sight? For in this way gold is beautiful too, possessing what attracts the eye and gives delight not from the symmetry of its parts, but from its good color alone.
orientation: Basil is explaining the meaning of the Spirit being borne upon the waters, then moves to God's first spoken command, 'Let there be light.'

title: Why the first day is called one, not first
english: And the evening star is the most beautiful of the stars, not because its parts are in proportion to one another, but because its radiance falls on the eyes in a way that is painless and pleasant. Then again, God's judgment about the beautiful was made not only with a view to what delights the sight, but also with foresight of the benefit that would come from it later. For there were as yet no eyes to judge the beauty in light. And God separated between the light and between the darkness (Genesis 1:4). That is, God made their natures unmixed and opposed to one another in contrariety. For he set them apart and divided them by the greatest distance.

And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night (Genesis 1:5). Now, after the creation of the sun, day is the air lit by the sun when it shines in the hemisphere above the earth, and night is the shadow of the earth that occurs when the sun is hidden. But then it was not according to the sun's movement; rather, as that firstborn light was poured forth and again contracted according to the measure fixed by God, day came to be, and night followed in turn. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day (Genesis 1:5). Evening, then, is the common boundary of day and night; and morning likewise is the neighborhood of night to day. So in order to give the privileges of birth to the day, he first named the end of the day, and then the end of the night, since night follows after day. For the state of the world before the creation of light was not night, but darkness; what was set in contrast to the day was named night, and it received this newer name after the day. So there was evening, and there was morning. He means the day-night. And he no longer named them day and night, but assigned the whole name to the prevailing one. You would find this same custom throughout all Scripture: in the measuring of time, days are counted, and not nights along with the days. The days of our years, says the psalmist (Psalm 89:10 LXX, Hebrew 90:10). And again Jacob: The days of my life are few and evil (Genesis 47:9). And again: All the days of my life (Psalm 26:4 LXX, Hebrew 27:4). So what has now been handed down in the form of history is legislation for what follows. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day (Genesis 1:5). Why did he not say first, but one? And yet it would have been more consistent for the one who was about to bring in a second, third, and fourth day to call the day that begins the sequence first. But he said one, either defining the boundary of the measure of day and night and joining together the time of the day-night, since the twenty-four hours complete the interval of one day—night being clearly included along with the day—so that even if at the turnings of the sun one of them happens to exceed the other, the intervals of both are nevertheless always circumscribed within the appointed time. It is as if he were saying: the measure of twenty-four hours is the interval of one day; or, the return of the heaven from the same point to the same point again happens in one day. So however often evening and morning overtake the world according to the sun's circuit, the period is completed not in more time, but in the interval of one day.
orientation: Basil is explaining Genesis 1:5, arguing that God's judgment that light was good looked to future benefit, and that the first day is called 'one' to define the measure of a day-night cycle.

title: Why the first day is called 'one' not 'first'
english: Or perhaps the more authoritative account is the one handed down in secret: that the God who fashioned the nature of time imposed measures and signs upon it—the intervals of days—and measuring it by the week, he commands the week always to return in a circle upon itself, counting out the movement of time. And the week, in turn, is completed by one day, returning upon itself seven times—and this is a circular shape, to begin from itself and end in itself. This is also the special property of eternity: to return upon itself and never come to an end. For this reason he named the head of time not “first day” but “one day,” so that even from the name it would have kinship with eternity. For the name that displays the character of what is solitary and unshared with another was fittingly and properly called “one.” And if Scripture presents many ages to us, speaking in many places of “age of age” and “ages of ages,” yet even there no first or second or third age has been counted out for us—so that from this we are shown differences of various conditions and affairs, not boundaries and limits and successions of ages. For “the day of the Lord,” it says, “is great and glorious” (Joel 2:11). And again, “Why do you seek the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18). Darkness, clearly, for those who deserve the darkness. For the word knows that day to be without evening, without succession, and without end—the day the psalmist also called the eighth, because it lies outside this sevenfold time. So whether you say “day” or “age,” you will mean the same thing. If that condition is called a day, it is one and not many; if it is called an age, it is solitary and not one of many. So to lead our thought toward the life to come, he named the image of eternity “one”—the firstfruits of days, the same age as the light, the holy Lord’s day, honored by the resurrection of the Lord. “And there was evening,” it says, “and there was morning, one day” (Genesis 1:5). But the words about that evening have been overtaken by the present evening, and here they bring our discourse to a close. May the Father of the true light, who adorned the day with heavenly light, who brightened the night with the rays of fire, who prepared the rest of the coming age with the spiritual and unceasing light, enlighten your hearts in the knowledge of the truth, and keep your life without stumbling, granting us to walk becomingly as in the day, so that you may shine like the sun in the brightness of the saints, for my boast, for the day of Christ—to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
HOMILY 3. On the Firmament.

The works of the first day—or rather, of the one day; for let us not take away from it the dignity it has in its nature, given by the Creator as a day in its own right, not numbered in sequence with the others—the things that came to be on it, then, our discourse went through yesterday and divided the explanation among the hearers, making the morning food for souls and the evening gladness. Now it moves on to the wonders of the second day.
orientation: Basil is expounding the first day of creation and explaining why Scripture calls it 'one day' rather than 'first day'.

title: The Word of God and the Firmament's Purpose
english: I say this not to point to the power of the one expounding, but to the grace of what is written, which by its nature is readily received and is gentle and dear to every heart among those who prize truth above persuasion. The psalmist shows this sweetness that comes from truth most emphatically when he says, “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118:103 (LXX; Hebrew 119:103)). Yesterday, then, as far as we could, we gladdened your souls by dwelling on the words of God, and today we have met again on the second day to behold the wonders of the second day’s works. But I have not failed to notice that many craftsmen of the manual trades, who lovingly earn their food from their daily labor, have surrounded us and are shortening our discourse so that they are not drawn away from their work for long. What do I say to them? That the portion of time lent to God is not lost, but is repaid by him with great interest. For whatever circumstances produce distraction, the Lord will let these pass by, giving bodily strength, eagerness of soul, ease in dealings, and prosperity through the whole of life to those who make spiritual things their priority. And even if in the present our earnest efforts do not turn out according to our hopes, still for the age to come the teaching of the Spirit is a good treasure. So remove from your heart every care of life, and gather all of yourself here to me. For there is not any benefit in the body’s being present while your heart labors over an earthly treasure.

And God said, “Let a firmament come into being in the midst of the water, and let it separate water from water” (Genesis 1:6). Yesterday we already heard the words of God: “Let light come into being” (Genesis 1:3). And today: “Let a firmament come into being.” But the present words seem to have something more, because the word did not remain in the bare command alone, but also defined in addition the reason for which the construction of the firmament is required. “So that it may separate,” he says, “between water and water.” First, then, let us take up the question of how God speaks. Is it in our manner—first the impression from things arises in the understanding, then after imagining it, he selects from the underlying realities the proper and fitting signs of each and declares them, then hands over what has been understood to the service of the vocal organs, and so through the impression made on the air, by the articulate movement of the voice, makes the thought known secretly? And how is it not mythical to say that God needs such a roundabout way for the declaration of what he has understood? Or is it more reverent to say that the divine will and the first impulse of the intellectual movement—this is the Word of God? Scripture shapes him in a discursive way in order to show that he not only willed the creation to come into being, but also that it was brought into being through some co-worker. For it could have, as it said from the beginning, gone through all things: “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1); then, “He made light”; then, “He made the firmament.” But now, by introducing God commanding and speaking, it hints at the one to whom he commands and to whom he speaks, in what is left silent—not begrudging us the knowledge, but kindling us toward desire, through the traces and indications it suggests of the ineffable.
orientation: Basil is opening his third homily, on the firmament, and has just addressed the crowd, including artisans who want him to keep the sermon short.

title: The purpose of God's spoken word and the question of multiple heavens
english: What is gained by labor is received with great joy and guarded with diligence, while what comes easily is held cheaply. For this reason Scripture leads us forward by a kind of path and order toward the knowledge of the only Son. And yet the incorporeal nature had no need of spoken words even so, since the very things conceived could be communicated directly to the co-worker. What need would there be for speech among those who can share their counsels with one another from the thought itself? For voice exists for hearing, and hearing for voice. But where there is no air, no tongue, no ear, no winding passage carrying sounds up to the perception in the head, there is no need of words either; the intention is communicated, one might say, from the very thoughts in the heart. So, as I said, this form of discourse has been wisely and skillfully employed in order to rouse our minds to search for the person to whom the words are addressed.

The second question to examine is whether this firmament, which was itself also called heaven, is different from the heaven made in the beginning, and whether there are in fact two heavens. The philosophers of heaven would sooner surrender their tongues than accept this as true. They posit one heaven, and say it has no nature capable of admitting a second, or third, or many more, since all the substance of the heavenly body was used up, as they think, in the constitution of the one. For they say there is one revolving body, and it is finite; and if this was completely fitted together with the first heaven, nothing is left over for the generation of a second or third. These are the imaginings of those who introduce unbegotten matter to the Creator, carried from their first myth-making into the falsehood that follows from it. But we ask the wise men of the Greeks not to mock us before they settle their disputes with one another. For among them there are some who say the heavens and worlds are infinite; and when those who use weightier proofs refute their implausibility and establish by geometric necessities that no other heaven can by nature come into being besides the one, then we will laugh all the more at their geometric and artful nonsense—if, seeing bubbles produced by the same cause, one and many alike, they still doubt about multiple heavens, whether the creative power suffices to bring them into being. When we look to the surpassing power of God, we consider the strength and magnitude of these heavens to differ in no way from the hollow moisture blown up in fountains. So their argument from impossibility is laughable. We, however, are so far from disbelieving in the second that we seek also the third, the vision of which the blessed Paul was counted worthy to receive. And the psalm, naming the heavens of heavens (Psalm 148:4), has given us the idea of still more. Surely these things are no more extraordinary than the seven circles, on which nearly all agree the seven stars are carried, and which they say are fitted one into another, like the image of jars set inside one another. These, moving in a direction opposite to the whole, while the ether is parted by them, produce a clear and harmonious sound, surpassing every pleasure found in melodies.
orientation: Basil is explaining why Genesis presents God as speaking during creation, then turns to ask whether the firmament is a second heaven distinct from the one made in the beginning.

title: The firmament's nature and the water above it
english: Then, when those who say these things are asked for the proof of sense perception, what do they answer? They say that because we have been accustomed to the sound from our first origin and have grown used to it from the beginning, we have lost the perception of it through long practice in hearing it—just like people in bronze workshops who have their ears struck continually. To refute the sophistry and rottenness of this argument, which is so plainly evident to everyone at first hearing, is not the work of a man who knows how to spare time or who aims at the understanding of his hearers. But let us leave the things of outsiders to outsiders and return to the ecclesiastical discourse.

Some of those before us have said that this is not the creation of a second heaven, but a further explanation of the first, because there the making of heaven and earth was handed down in summary, while here the Scripture hands down to us in more detailed fashion the manner in which each thing came to be. But we say that since a different name and a special function of the second heaven have been handed down, this one is other than the one made in the beginning, of a firmer nature, and providing an exceptional service to the whole.

And God said, “Let a firmament come into being in the midst of the water, and let it be separating between water and water.” And God made the firmament, and God separated between the water that was beneath the firmament and between the water that was above the firmament (Genesis 1:6-7). But before we touch the meaning of what is written, let us try to dissolve the objection brought against us by others. For they ask us: if the body of the firmament is spherical, as sight shows, and water is fluid and slips off high places, how could it have been made to sit firmly on the curved surface of the firmament? What then shall we say to this? That it is not at all necessary that what appears circular to us in its inner concavity should also have its outer surface finished spherically, and be perfectly turned and smoothly rounded throughout. For we see the stone roofs of baths and the construction of cave-like buildings, which are rounded into a semicircular shape on the inner view, yet often have a flat surface on the top of the roof. So for this reason let them neither make trouble for themselves nor cause trouble for us, as though we could not hold the water in the upper regions.

Next it would be right to say what the nature of the firmament is, and for what reason it was appointed to mediate between the waters. The name “firmament” is customary in Scripture for things that excel in strength. For example, when it says, “The Lord is my firmament and my refuge” (Psalm 17:3 LXX [Hebrew 18:2]), and “I have made firm its pillars” (Psalm 74:4 LXX [Hebrew 75:3]), and “Praise him in the firmament of his power” (Psalm 150:1 LXX [Hebrew 150:1]). Those outside call a solid body something dense and full, which is said in contrast to the mathematical. The mathematical is that which has its being only in dimensions—in breadth, I mean, and depth and height—while the solid is that which has resistance in addition to the dimensions. But it is customary for Scripture to call what is strong and unyielding a firmament, as it often uses this word even of air that has been greatly condensed, as when it says, “He who makes firm the thunder” (Job 37:4 LXX [Hebrew 37:4]).
orientation: Basil is expounding the second day of creation, answering objections about how water can rest on the curved firmament and explaining what Scripture means by 'firmament.'

title: The firmament is solid but not ice or crystal
english: Scripture speaks of the solidity and resistance of the wind that is caught in the hollows of the clouds. When that wind bursts out violently, it produces the sounds of thunder. Scripture called this force the making firm of thunder (Amos 4:13). Basil says we hold that this utterance about the firmament has been appointed for a different purpose: for a solid nature strong enough to hold back what is slippery and easily dissolved in water.

That does not mean we should suppose the firmament looks like frozen water, merely because the common view holds that it takes its origin from water. Nor should we suppose it is made of some matter that begins when moisture is filtered, like crystal stone or like the mica that forms in mines. People say water is changed into crystal stone by extreme freezing. Mica is a transparent stone with its own very pure clearness. If a piece is found true to its nature, neither eaten away by any decay nor split through its depth by cracks, its brightness is almost like air. Basil says we liken the firmament to none of these things. To hold such notions about heaven is truly the mark of a childish and simple mind. It is true that all things are in all things: fire is in earth, air is in water, and each of the other elements is likewise in another. None of the elements perceived by the senses is pure and unmixed, whether by sharing in what tends toward the middle or in what tends toward its opposite. For that reason Basil says we do not accept saying that the firmament either comes from one of the simple elements or is a mixture made from them. Scripture has taught us to allow our minds to imagine nothing beyond what has been granted.

Basil says we should not pass over one point without marking it. After God gave the command, “Let there be a firmament” (Genesis 1:6), Scripture does not simply add, “and there was a firmament.” It says instead, “And God made the firmament” (Genesis 1:7), and again, “God divided.” Scripture says, “You deaf, hear, and you blind, look up” (Isaiah 42:18). Basil asks who is deaf except the one who does not hear the Spirit crying out so loudly. And who is blind except the one who does not see such clear proofs concerning the only Son. “Let there be a firmament” is the voice of the preliminary cause. “God made the firmament” bears witness to his making and fashioning power.

But Basil says let us return our speech to the course of the explanation. God says, “Let it be dividing between water and water” (Genesis 1:6). The outpouring of the waters was boundless, it seems, surging over the earth from every side and hanging above it, so that it seemed to exceed its due proportion to the other elements. For this reason it was said earlier that the earth was clothed all around by the deep. Basil says he will give the reason for this abundance later. Certainly none of you will object to this account as if it assumed impossible or invented things, not even those among you whose minds are highly trained and keenly observant of this perishable and fleeting nature. Nor will you demand from us an account of what the nature of the waters rested upon. By the same reasoning by which they hold the earth suspended in the middle, though it is heavier than water, drawing it away from the outermost bounds, they will surely also grant that the countless water rests motionless around the earth, both because it naturally moves downward and because it is evenly balanced on every side.
orientation: Basil is explaining the firmament God commands on the second day to divide water from water.

title: Why the waters were created in such abundance
english: So the boundless nature of the water had been poured around the earth, not in proportion to it, but exceeding it many times over. From the beginning the great craftsman foresaw what was to come and arranged the first things for the need that would follow. What need was there, then, for the water to exceed by an unspeakable amount? Because the substance of fire is necessary to the whole—not only for the ordering of things around the earth, but also for the completion of the universe. For the whole would have been maimed if it lacked the one greatest and most vital element of all. These two are opposed to each other, and each is destructive of the other: fire destroys water when it prevails by force, and water destroys fire when it exceeds in quantity. But there had to be neither a standoff between them nor any occasion given to the universe for dissolution through the complete failure of one of them. The One who orders all things arranged in advance such a quantity of the moist nature that, as it is gradually consumed by the power of fire, it would hold out until the appointed limits of the world's duration. For the One who arranged all things by weight and measure—since, according to Job, even the drops of rain are numbered by him (Job 38:37 (LXX))—knew how much time he had marked off for the world to endure, and how much expenditure he needed to set aside in advance for the fire. This is the reason for the abundance of water at creation.

But surely no one is so entirely outside of life as to need instruction from this discourse that fire is necessary to the world. Not only because all the crafts that sustain our lives require the work of fire—I mean weaving, leather-working, building, and farming—but because neither the sprouting of trees, nor the ripening of fruits, nor the generation of land animals or water creatures, nor their nourishment, would ever have come into being in the beginning or endured over time if heat were absent. So the creation of heat is necessary for the formation and continuance of things that come into being, and the abundance of moisture is necessary because the consumption of fire is unceasing and unavoidable.

Look around at the whole creation, and you will see the power of heat ruling over everything that comes into being and decays. For this reason much water was poured over the earth, carried beyond the visible regions, and in addition sown throughout the entire depth of the earth. From there come abundant springs, the gathering of wells, the streams of rivers—both winter torrents and ever-flowing ones—so that the moisture is preserved in many and varied storehouses. From the east, from the winter solstice, flows the Indus River, the greatest stream of all river waters, as those who have written accounts of the earth's regions have recorded. From the middle of the east flow the Bactrus, the Choaspes, and the Araxes, from which the Tanais branches off and empties into the Sea of Azov. And besides these, the Phasis flows down from the Caucasus Mountains, and countless other rivers from the northern regions rush toward the Black Sea. From the west, from the summer solstice, beneath the Pyrenees, flow the Tartessus and the Ister. One of these pours into the sea beyond the Pillars of Hercules, while the Ister flows through Europe and empties into the Black Sea.
orientation: Basil is explaining why the earth was initially covered with far more water than it needed, arguing that the excess was stored up to fuel the sun's fire over the whole duration of the world.

title: Rivers and the fiery heaven: why water abounds
english: And why should I list the rest of the rivers born from the Rhipaean mountains, the heights beyond the innermost part of Scythia? Among them is the Rhone, along with countless other rivers, themselves navigable, which pass by the western Gauls and Celts and the barbarians bordering them, and all pour into the western sea. Others come from the south, from above through Ethiopia: some flow toward our sea, while others empty into the sea beyond the one that is sailed. There are the Aegon, the Nyses, and the one called Chremetes, and besides these the Nile, whose nature is not even like that of rivers when it floods Egypt like a sea. So the region of our inhabited world is surrounded by water, bound by immense seas and watered by countless ever-flowing rivers, through the ineffable wisdom of the One who arranged that the nature opposed to fire should be hard to consume.
