Yet there will come a time when all things will be burned up by fire, as Isaiah says in the words he addresses to the God of all: 'He who says to the deep, You shall be made desolate, and I will dry up all your rivers' (Isaiah 44:27). Therefore cast away the wisdom that has become foolish, and accept with us the teaching of truth, plain in its speech but infallible in its knowledge.

For this reason: 'Let a firmament come into being in the midst of the water, and let it separate water from water' (Genesis 1:6). We have already said what the name 'firmament' means in Scripture. It does not mean a resistant and solid nature, one that has weight and offers resistance—Scripture does not call that a firmament. If it did, the earth would more properly have been given that name. But because the nature of the things above is fine and loose and not graspable by any sense, Scripture named it 'firmament' by comparison with the finest things that are imperceptible to the senses. And understand it as a place that separates the moist element: the fine and filtered part passes through to the upper regions, while the thickest and earthiest part is released below, so that from beginning to end the same good temperature may be preserved, as the moist elements are gradually drawn off in part. But you distrust the abundance of water, while you do not consider the abundance of heat—which, even if small in size, is capable of consuming a great deal of moisture because of its power. For it draws in the moisture that lies near it, as the cupping glass shows; and it consumes what it has drawn in, like the fire of a lamp, which draws up the fuel that lies near it through the wick and quickly turns it to ash through the change. And who doubts that the ether is fiery and burning hot? If it were not held back by the necessary limit set by its Maker, what would prevent it from setting everything ablaze and burning up all that is near it, consuming at once all the moisture in all things? For this reason there is aerial water, as the upper region becomes cloudy from the rising of vapors that rivers and springs and marshes and lakes and seas all send forth, so that the ether may not seize everything and set it on fire. Indeed, we see this very sun, in the summer season, often leaving a soaked and marshy land completely dry and parched in the briefest moment of time.
orientation: Basil is still cataloguing the rivers of the world and now turns to explain why the earth is so abundantly watered, arguing that water tempers the fiery nature of the upper region.

title: The sun's heat and the naming of the firmament
english: Where then is that water? Let those who are clever in all things show us. Is it not obvious to everyone that it was cut through by the heat of the sun and used up? And yet those same people say the sun is not even hot—so much surplus of speaking is theirs. Consider what kind of proof they rely on when they oppose what is plainly evident. Because the sun is white in color, they say, and not reddish or yellow, for this reason it is not fiery in nature; but its heat, they say, comes from its rapid rotation. What do they gain for themselves by this? That the sun should not seem to consume any of the waters. For my part, even if what they say is not true, I do not reject it, since it helps to build my argument. For it was said that the abundance of waters was necessary because of the consumption caused by heat. And it makes no difference whether the sun is hot by nature or has its burning from an acquired condition, at least as far as producing the same results in the same materials. For whether wood rubbed together kindles fire and flame, or whether it is burned up by a kindled flame, the end from both is equal and alike. And indeed we see the great wisdom of him who governs all things, moving the sun from one region to another, so that by not always lingering upon the same places it may not damage the ordered arrangement by the excess of heat; but now he leads it toward the southern region at the winter solstice, now moves it to the equinoctial points, and from there brings it back toward the north at the summer solstice, so that by its gradual movement the good temperature of the region around the earth may be preserved. Let them consider whether they do not contradict themselves—they who say that the sea is not made to overflow by the rivers because of the sun's consumption, and moreover that it is left salty and bitter because the fine and drinkable part is used up by the heat; which happens especially from the separation accomplished by the sun, drawing off the light part and causing the thick and earthy part to settle like some mud and sediment; from this the bitter and salty and drying quality belongs to the sea. Those who say these things about the sea, turning around again, say that no diminution of moisture comes from the sun. And God called the firmament heaven (Genesis 1:8)—the name properly belongs to another, but this also shares in the title by way of likeness. We have observed that in many places the visible region is called heaven, because the solid and continuous air clearly falls under our sight, and because it is seen it is deemed worthy of the name of heaven; as in the words, The birds of heaven (Genesis 1:26). And again: The things that fly across the firmament of heaven (Genesis 1:20). Of this kind also is the saying, They go up to the heavens. And Moses, blessing the tribe of Joseph, gives blessings from the seasons of heaven and the dew, and from the sun's turnings and the meetings of months, and from the tops of mountains and everlasting hills (Deuteronomy 33:13-15), since the region around the earth is made fruitful through the good order in these things. But also in the curses upon Israel he says, The heaven over your head shall be bronze (Deuteronomy 28:23).
orientation: Basil is answering opponents who deny that the sun is hot, then turns to the naming of the firmament as heaven.

title: Literal water above the firmament, not spiritual powers
english: What does he mean by this? He means complete dryness and the failure of the waters in the air, through which the earth has its power to bear fruit. So when he says that dew or rain is carried from heaven, we understand it as the waters that have been appointed to occupy the upper region. For when the exhalations gather in the heights, and the air is compressed by the force of the winds, the moisture that until then was scattered through the cloud in vapor-like, fine particles draws together, and drops form, carried downward by the weight of what has collected—and this is how rain comes to be. But when the moisture is made to foam, beaten back by the violence of the winds, and then is chilled to the utmost and frozen through and through, the cloud breaks apart and snow falls down. In short, by the same principle you can observe the whole nature of moisture taking shape in the air above our heads.

And let no one compare the simple and unadorned character of the spiritual words with the over-curious speculations of those who have philosophized about the heavens. For as much as the beauty of a chaste woman is to be preferred to that of a courtesan, so great is the difference between our words and those from outside. Those men impose a forced plausibility on their arguments; here the truth lies open, stripped of artifice. And why should we trouble ourselves to refute their falsehood, when it is enough to set their own books against one another and sit quietly as spectators of their war? For they are neither fewer in number nor inferior in rank, but they stand opposed to one another with great many-voicedness, some saying that the universe is consumed by fire and comes to life again from the seminal principles that remain in the burned remains—which is how they introduce endless destructions of the world and rebirths. But those men, splitting away from the truth on both sides, discover for themselves the paths of error in every direction.

But we also have a word to address to those from the Church concerning the separated waters—those who, on the pretext of anagogy and higher thoughts, have fled to allegories, saying that spiritual and incorporeal powers are figuratively signified by the waters: that the better powers remained above on the firmament, while the evil ones stayed below in the earthly and material regions. For this reason, they say, the waters above the heavens praise God—that is, the good powers, being worthy through the purity of their governing part, render fitting praise to the Creator. But the waters below the heavens, they say, are the spiritual powers of wickedness, which fell from their natural height into the depth of evil. Because they are turbulent and rebellious and tossed by the disturbances of the passions, they were named 'sea' on account of the changeableness and instability of their movements of choice.

Let us send such arguments away as comparisons of dreams and old wives' tales, and let us understand water as water, and let us accept the separation made by the firmament according to the reason already given. And indeed, even if the waters above the heavens are sometimes taken up for the praise of the common Lord of all, we do not therefore assign them a rational nature. For the heavens are not ensouled just because they declare the glory of God (Psalm 18:2 LXX), nor is the firmament a living, perceiving creature just because it announces the work of his hands (Psalm 18:2 LXX).
orientation: Basil is explaining the waters above the firmament from Genesis 1:6-7 and rejecting allegorical readings that turn them into spiritual powers.

title: Literal sense defended; God approves each work as good
english: If someone says that the heavens are the contemplative powers and the firmament is the practical and productive powers concerned with duties, we accept the argument as elegant, but we will not at all grant that it is true. For by that logic dew, frost, cold, and heat—since they were commanded in Daniel to hymn the creator of all things—would be some intelligent and invisible nature. But when thoughtful people interpret the language in these passages with discernment, it is a completion of the praise of the creator. For not only does the water above the heavens fulfill its praise to God, as holding first place in honor because of the superiority it possesses from virtue, but, as it says, 'Praise him, also the things from the earth, dragons and all deeps' (Psalm 148:7). So even the deep, which the allegorizers cast away into the worse portion, was not judged rejectable by the psalmist, but was received into the common chorus of creation; and it too, according to the principles inherent in it, harmoniously completes the hymn to its maker.

And God saw that it was good. The things made by God do not provide pleasure to God's eyes, nor is his acceptance of good things the same as ours. Rather, what is good is what has been completed by the principle of his art and what conduces to the useful service of its purpose. So the one who set before himself the clear goal of the things being made, and who examined each thing made in its parts as contributing to the completion of that end by his own artistic principles, approved them. After all, a hand by itself, an eye on its own, and each of the limbs of a statue lying separately would not appear beautiful to just anyone; but when they are set in their proper order, the beauty that comes from proportion becomes evident, even to the untrained eye, though only with difficulty. The craftsman, however, knows the beauty of each part even before the composition, and he praises each individual part, referring his thought back to their end. Such, then, is the kind of artistic praiser of the individual works that God is now recorded to be; and he is going to complete the fitting praise also for the whole world together when it is finished.

But let our words about the second day come to an end here, so as to give the diligent hearers time to examine what they have heard, so that if there is anything useful in it, they may hold it fast in memory, and through diligent meditation—as through a kind of digestion—await the distribution of what is beneficial. And for those occupied with the affairs of life, let this interval give them leisure to set their cares in order, so that with a soul cleansed of anxieties they may come to the evening feast of words. May the God who created the great things and who has arranged for these small things to be spoken give you understanding in all his truth, so that from the things that are seen you may perceive the invisible, and from the greatness and beauty of the creatures you may take up the fitting glory concerning the one who created us. For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world by the things made, are clearly seen, both his eternal power and divinity (Romans 1:20), so that in earth, in air, in heaven, in water, in night, in day, and in all things visible, we may receive clear reminders of our benefactor.
orientation: Basil is closing Homily 3 on the firmament, rejecting allegorical readings of the waters above and explaining why God saw that the work was good.

title: The soul's theatre versus God's workshop
english: For we will give no occasion to sins, nor will we leave any place for the enemy in our hearts, since through constant remembrance we have God dwelling within us. To him be all glory and worship, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Homily 4: On the gathering of the waters

There are some cities that feast the eyes with all kinds of spectacles by wonder-workers from early dawn until evening itself. And indeed, though they listen at great length to certain broken and corrupted melodies that plant every kind of wantonness in the soul, they are never filled. Many count such crowds blessed, because they abandon the business of the marketplace and the crafts devised for making a living, and pass through the appointed time of their life in complete ease and pleasure. They do not know that a theatre flourishing with licentious spectacles is a common and public school of wantonness for those who sit together in it, and that the harmonious melodies of the flutes and the songs of wantonness, sitting in the souls of those who hear them, persuade everyone to behave shamefully, imitating the strumming of the harpists or the flute-players. And already some of the horse-mad even fight about horses in their dreams, re-yoking chariots and changing charioteers, and in the fantasies of sleep they do not depart at all from their daytime folly.

But shall we, whom the Lord, the great wonder-worker and craftsman, has summoned to the display of his own works, grow weary of the sight, or shrink from hearing the words of the Spirit? Rather, let us stand around this great and varied workshop of the divine creation, and let each of us return in thought to the ancient times, and shall we not see the ordering of the universe: heaven standing, according to the prophetic word, like a vault; the earth, infinite in size and weight, fixed upon itself; air poured out, soft and moist by nature, providing a proper and constant nourishment to those who breathe, yielding and parting before those who move through it because of its softness, so that it offers no obstacle to those who rush forward, always flowing around to meet from behind those who cut through it. And the nature of water, prepared for us both for nourishment and for other uses, and its orderly gathering into the appointed places, you will see from what has just been read to us.

And God said, 'Let the water under heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.' And it was so, and the water under heaven was gathered into their gatherings, and the dry land appeared. And God called the dry land earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called seas (Genesis 1:9-10).

How much trouble you gave me in the previous words, demanding the reason why the earth was invisible, since color is naturally present with every body, and every color is perceptible to sight! And perhaps what was said did not seem sufficient to you: that 'invisible' was said with reference to us, not with reference to its nature, because of the covering of water that then concealed all the earth. See now, hear the Scripture itself revealing itself.
orientation: Basil has just closed the third homily with a prayer and now opens the fourth homily, contrasting the empty spectacles of the cities with the spectacle of God's creation that Scripture sets before his hearers.

title: Why God commanded the waters to gather
english: 'Let the waters be gathered, and let the dry land appear' (Genesis 1:9). The curtains are drawn together, so that what was previously unseen may become visible. Perhaps someone might seek in addition this further point. First, why does the account attribute to the command of the Creator what belongs to water by nature—its movement toward a downward slope? For as long as water happens to lie on level ground, it is still, having nowhere to flow. But when it takes hold of some downward incline, when the leading water rushes forward, the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved, and the following water seizes the base of that one. And so the leading water always escapes from under, while the water coming after pushes it on. And the flow becomes swifter the greater the weight of what is carried down and the deeper the hollow into which the influx runs. If water is like this by nature, then the command ordering it to be gathered into one gathering would be superfluous. For it was bound to run together of its own accord, because of the downward tendency of its nature, into the deepest region of all, and not to stop until its surface was leveled. For no place is as level as the surface of water. Then, someone says, how was the water commanded to run together into one gathering, when there are clearly many seas, separated from one another by great distances in their position? To the first of these questions we say this: you have come to know the movements of water after the Master's command—that it flows downward and is unstable, and is carried by nature toward slopes and hollows. But before that, what power it had before the course from this command was born in it, you neither saw yourself nor heard from anyone who saw. Understand that the voice of God is maker of nature, and the command given then to creation provided the continuity for what was created thereafter. Day and night were made once, and from that time until now they succeed one another and divide time in equal portions without ceasing. 'Let the waters be gathered.' The nature of the waters was commanded to run, and it never grows weary, urged on continually by that command. I say this with reference to the flowing portion of the waters. For some flow of their own accord, such as springs and rivers; others are artificially collected and without outlet. But my subject now is the rushing waters. 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.' If you have ever stood by a spring that sends up abundant water and wondered: Who is it that pushes this water from the flanks of the earth? Who urges it forward? What are the storehouses from which it comes? What is the place to which it hurries? How is it that these do not fail, and those are not filled up? All this depends on that first voice. From there the water received the signal to run. In every account of waters, remember the first voice: 'Let the waters be gathered.' They had to run, so that each might reach its proper place; then, having come into the appointed regions, to remain by themselves and go no further. For this reason, according to the word of Ecclesiastes, 'All the torrents go to the sea, and the sea is not filled' (Ecclesiastes 1:7).
orientation: Basil is answering objections about God's command 'Let the waters be gathered' in Genesis 1:9, explaining why a command was needed for what seems natural to water.

title: The sea's boundary is God's command
english: The flowing of the waters and the sea's confinement within its boundaries both come from that first legislation: "Let the waters be gathered into one gathering" (Genesis 1:9). The water that kept flowing in would have overflowed the places that received it, always moving on and filling one place after another, until it flooded the whole continent in an unbroken sweep. So it was commanded to be gathered into one gathering. That is why the sea, even when it rages under the winds and its waves rear up to an enormous height, the moment it touches the shore, dissolves its force into foam and turns back. "Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea?" (Jeremiah 5:22). The sea, whose violence cannot be withstood, is bridled by the weakest thing of all—sand. What else kept the Red Sea from sweeping over all Egypt, which lies lower than the sea itself, and joining the ocean that borders Egypt, if it was not bound by the command of its Creator? That Egypt is lower than the Red Sea has been proved to us in practice by those who wanted to join the two seas to each other—the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, in which the Red Sea lies. That is why they abandoned the attempt: first Sesostris the Egyptian, who began it, and then Darius the Mede, who later wanted to carry it through. I have said all this so that we may understand the power of the command: "Let the waters be gathered into one gathering." That is, let no other gathering be produced from this one, but let what is gathered remain in that first collection.

Then the one who said that the waters should be gathered into one gathering showed you that the waters had been many, divided among many places. The hollows of the mountains, split by deep ravines, held their own collections of water. And in addition, many broad and level plains, no smaller in extent than the greatest seas, and countless valleys and basins hollowed out in every kind of shape—all of them, filled with water at that time, were emptied by the divine command, as the water from every direction was driven together into one gathering. And let no one say: if there was water above the earth, then surely all the hollows that now hold the sea must already have been full. Where, then, were the gatherings of the waters going to form, if the hollows were already occupied? To this we will answer that the vessels were prepared at that very time, when the water had to be set apart into one mass. For the sea beyond Cadiz did not yet exist, nor that great ocean untried by sailors, which embraces the island of Britain and the western Iberians. But at that time, when the wide expanse was created by God's command, the masses of water were gathered together into it.

As for the objection that our account of the world's making contradicts experience—since not all the water appears to have run together into one gathering—there is much to say, and it is obvious to everyone. Perhaps it is even ridiculous to argue against such objections. Surely they do not mean to bring up marsh water and rainwater collected in pools, and think they are refuting our argument with these? No, he called the greatest and most complete running together of the waters "one gathering."
orientation: Basil is expounding the command 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering' from Genesis 1:9, arguing that the sea's limits are fixed by divine decree, not by nature.

title: Lakes are gatherings but only the greatest water is seas
english: Even wells are man-made gatherings of waters. Moisture sown through the earth flows together into its hollowed place. So the title of gathering does not mean chance heaps of water. It means the outstanding and greatest gathering, in which the whole element appears together.

Fire is broken into small pieces for our use here, yet it pours together in full in the upper air. Air also divides into small portions, yet together it embraces the whole region around the earth. So it is with water. There are some small and divided formations, yet there is one gathering that separates the whole element from the rest.

The lakes are clearly gatherings of waters, both those in the northern regions and those around the Greek land, occupying Macedonia and Bithynia and Palestine. But my present subject is the greatest of them all, which rivals the earth itself in size. No one will deny that those lakes hold an abundance of water, yet no reasonable account would call them seas. This holds even if some have salt and an earthy quality like the great sea, such as the Asphaltitis lake in Judea and Serbonis between Egypt and Palestine, stretching alongside the Arabian desert. These are lakes, but the sea is one, as those who have traveled around the earth report. Even if some think the Caspian Sea lies enclosed by itself, if we must attend to the maps of those who have investigated, its parts break through to one another and all open together into the greatest sea. In the same way they say the Red Sea joins with the sea beyond Gadeira. At this point someone asks, “How then did God call the systems of the waters seas?” The waters did run together into one gathering. But the systems of the waters, that is, the gulfs cut off in their own shape by the surrounding land, these the Lord called seas. There is a northern sea and a southern sea, an eastern sea and another western one. The open seas also have their own names: the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara, the Dardanelles, the Aegean and the Ionian, the Sea of Sardinia and the Sea of Sicily, and another Tyrrhenian. There are countless names of the open seas, and to list them precisely now would be long and full of lack of taste.

For this reason God called the systems of the waters seas. The sequence of my argument has brought me to this point, but let me return to the beginning. And God said, “Let the waters be brought together into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:9). He did not say, “Let the earth appear.” He refused to display it again as unformed, since it lay as mud and mixed with water, and had not yet received its own form and power. At the same time the Creator made the dryness of the earth older than the birth of the sun, so that we would not assign to the sun the cause of drying the earth.

Fix your mind on what is written. Not only did the excess water flow off the earth. Whatever water had mixed with it through its depth also withdrew in obedience. It yielded to the compelling command of the Master.
orientation: Basil is continuing his literal exposition of the third day when God gathers the waters.

title: The dry land's proper quality and the naming of earth
english: “And it became so.” This sequel is sufficient to show that the Creator’s voice came to fulfillment in deed. But in many copies there is added: “And the water under heaven was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared”—which neither some of the other translators have published, nor does the usage of the Hebrews appear to contain. For in truth, after the testimony that “It became so,” the further detailed narration of the same things is redundant. In the accurate copies, then, these words have been marked with an obelus; and the obelus is a sign of rejection. “And God called the dry land earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called seas” (Genesis 1:10). Why is it that earlier it says, “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:9), but it is not written, “and let the earth appear”? And here again, “The dry land appeared, and God called the dry land earth”? Because “dry” is the peculiar property, the as it were characteristic of the nature of the underlying thing, while “earth” is a bare appellation of the thing. For just as rationality is the peculiar property of a human being, while the word “human being” signifies the animal in which that property resides, so also dryness is the peculiar and exceptional property of earth. That, then, which properly possesses dryness is called earth—just as that which properly possesses the neighing property is called a horse. And this is true not only of earth, but each of the other elements also has a peculiar and allotted quality, by which it is distinguished from the rest and by which each is recognized for what it is. Water has coldness as its own quality; air has moisture; fire has heat. But these, as the first elements of composite things, are contemplated by reason in the manner described; the things already arranged in body and falling under sense perception have their qualities joined together. And nothing among visible and perceptible things is absolutely single or simple and pure; rather, earth is dry and cold, water is moist and cold, air is hot and moist, fire is hot and dry. For in this way, through the paired quality, the power of each to mix with each comes forth. Each element is blended with its neighboring element through their common quality, and through its fellowship with what is near it is joined to its opposite. For example, earth, being dry and cold, is united to water through the kinship of coldness, and through water it is united to air; since water is placed in the middle between both, as if by the laying on of two hands it touches each of the adjacent elements with each quality—earth with its coldness, air with its moisture. Again, air by its own mediation becomes reconciler of the warring nature of water and fire, being intertwined with water through moisture and with fire through heat. And fire, being hot and dry in nature, is bound to air by its heat, and by its dryness it returns again to fellowship with earth.
orientation: Basil is explaining why Genesis says 'the dry land appeared' and then 'God called the dry land earth,' arguing that dryness is the defining quality of earth, and he extends this to the four elements and their paired qualities.

title: The circle of elements and the goodness of the sea
english: And so a circle and a harmonious dance comes into being, with all things in agreement and standing in order with one another. This is why the name “elements” is properly fitted to them. I have said all this to show the reason God called the dry land “earth,” but did not call the earth “dry land.” For dryness is not one of the things added to the earth later; it is one of the things that fill up its substance from the beginning. And the things that give it its cause of being are prior by nature and more honorable than the things added afterward. So it was reasonable that the earth’s distinguishing marks were conceived from what pre-existed and was older.

“And God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:10). The text does not mean that some pleasant sight of the sea appeared to God. For the Maker does not see the beauties of creation with eyes, but contemplates what comes into being with ineffable wisdom. A whitening sea is a sweet sight when a steady calm holds it; it is sweet too when its back is roughened by gentle breezes and it casts a purple or dark-blue color before those who watch—when it does not strike the neighboring land violently, but kisses it as if with peaceful embraces. But we must not think Scripture means that the sea appeared beautiful and sweet to God in this way. Rather, the good there is judged by the reasoning of the Creator's work.

First, the water of the sea is the source of all moisture around the earth. It is distributed through hidden channels, as the porous and cavernous places of the continents show. Beneath them the flowing sea runs in channels, and when it is caught in winding passages that do not run straight, it is pushed by the spirit that moves it, breaks through the surface, and flows outside—and becomes drinkable, its bitterness healed by the filtering. Sometimes it also takes on a hotter quality from metals along the way, and from the same cause that moves it, it often becomes boiling and fiery. This can be observed in many islands and many coastal places. Even inland, some places near river waters—to compare small things with great—suffer something similar. Why have I said this? Because all the earth is undermined, with water making its way beneath from the sources of the sea through hidden pores.

So the sea is good to God also because of the under-running of moisture in its depths. It is good also because it is the reservoir of rivers, receiving streams from everywhere into itself, and yet remains within its own boundaries. It is good also because it is a beginning and source for the waters in the air: it is warmed by the sun’s ray and sends off the fine part of the water through vapors. This is drawn up to the upper region, then cooled because it has risen higher than the reflection of the rays from the ground—and at the same time the shade from the cloud intensifies the cooling—and it becomes rain and enriches the earth. No one doubts these things who has considered heated cauldrons: full of liquid, they are often left empty when everything being boiled has been dispersed into vapor.
orientation: Basil is explaining why God called the dry land 'earth' rather than calling the earth 'dry,' and now turns to the meaning of 'And God saw that it was good' regarding the gathered waters.

title: The sea's beauty and the church's calm
english: You can also see the water of the sea being boiled by sailors: they catch the vapors with sponges and so relieve their need in emergencies, sufficiently. It is beautiful in another way in God's sight as well, because it encircles the islands, providing them at once with adornment and with safety through itself. Then too, because it joins together the continents that stand farthest apart from one another, offering sailors unhindered intercourse; through this it grants knowledge of things unknown, becomes a source of wealth for merchants, and easily supplies the needs of life, providing export for the surplus of those who abound and granting relief for the lack of those in need. And how could I see with precision the whole beauty of the sea, as much as appeared to the eye of its Maker? If the sea is beautiful and praiseworthy to God, how much more beautiful is the assembly of such a church, in which a mingled sound—like a wave breaking on the shore—is sent up from men and women and infants in their prayers to our God. A deep calm preserves it unshaken, since the spirits of wickedness have not been able to trouble it with heretical words. May you then become worthy of the Lord's approval, preserving this good order in the most fitting way, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
HOMILY 5: On the Sprouting of the Earth

And God said, "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, seed-bearing according to kind, and the fruit tree producing fruit according to kind, whose seed is in it" (Genesis 1:11). It follows that after the earth had rested, having put off the weight of the water, the command came to it to sprout first herb, then tree—which we still see happening now. For that voice then, and that first command, became like a law of nature and remained in the earth, granting it the power to generate and bear fruit for the time to come. "Let the earth sprout." First in the generation of growing things is the sprouting; then, when the sprouts come up a little, herb appears; then, when it has grown, it is grass, as the growing things are gradually articulated and advance to the completion of the seed. For the green and grassy state is similar in all of them. "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass." Let the earth bring forth the sprouting by itself, needing no cooperation from any other source. Since some people think the sun is the cause of the things that grow from the earth, drawing up the power from the depths to the surface by the attraction of heat, for this reason the ordering of the earth is older than the sun—so that those who have gone astray may stop worshiping the sun as though it provided the cause of life. If they are persuaded that everything concerning the earth was ordered before the sun's creation, they will also let go of their excessive wonder at it, considering that it is younger than grass and herb in its origin. Was food then laid out beforehand for the cattle, while our own provision appeared worthy of no forethought? But surely the one who stored up fodder for cattle and horses beforehand is above all preparing wealth and enjoyment for you.
orientation: Basil is concluding his praise of the sea's usefulness and beauty, then turns to praise the gathered church and introduces the fifth homily on vegetation.

title: Seed and succession in plants
english: For the one who feeds your flocks is also building up the provision for your own life. And then, what is the origin of seeds if not a preparation for your way of living? Besides, many of the things that are still among grasses and garden herbs serve as food for human beings. "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, sowing seed," it says, "according to kind" (Genesis 1:11). So even if some kind of herb differs from others, its benefit comes back to us, and the use of the seeds is set apart for us. The meaning of the words, then, is this: "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, and seed sowing according to kind." In this way the sequence of the wording can be restored—since the syntax now seems inconsistent—and the necessary order of what nature arranges will be preserved. For first comes sprouting, then the green shoot, then the growth of the grass, then the completion of what grows through the seed. How then, they say, does the text show that everything growing from the earth has seed, when neither reed nor couch grass nor mint, not crocus, not garlic, not sedge, nor countless other kinds of plants appear to produce seed? To this we answer that many of the things growing from the earth have the power of their seeds in the base and the root. Just as the reed, after its yearly growth, sends out from the root a certain shoot having the principle of seed for the future. Countless other plants do the same, all that spread through the ground and possess their succession in their roots. So it is truer than anything that for each thing that grows there is either a seed or some seedlike power existing within it. And this is what "according to kind" means. For the shoot of the reed does not produce an olive tree, but from a reed comes another reed, and from seeds the things related to what was sown spring up. And so what the earth brought forth in the first creation is preserved even until now, the kind being guarded by the sequence of succession. "Let the earth sprout." Consider for me how from a small utterance and so brief a command, the frozen and barren earth suddenly travails and is stirred toward fruit-bearing, as though throwing off a gloomy and mournful garment and clothing herself in a brighter one, rejoicing in her proper ornaments and putting forth the countless kinds of growing things. I want the wonder of creation to be fixed in you more intensely, so that wherever you find yourself, and whatever kind of growing thing you stand beside, you may receive a vivid reminder of the Maker. First, then, when you see the herb of grass and a flower, bring to mind human nature, remembering the image of the wise Isaiah, that "All flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass" (Isaiah 40:6). For the brevity of life, and the short-lived joy and brightness of human prosperity, has found in the prophet a most fitting image. Today a man flourishes in body, fleshed out by luxury, with his good color blooming from the prime of his age, vigorous and taut and irresistible in impulse; tomorrow this same man is pitiable, either withered by time or dissolved by disease.
orientation: Basil is explaining Genesis 1:11, arguing that every plant has seed or a seedlike power, and then turns to the moral lesson of grass and flower as an image of human frailty.

title: The fleeting glory of the powerful and the ordered growth of plants
english: One man is admired for his abundance of wealth. Around him is a crowd of flatterers, a bodyguard of pretended friends who court his favor, a host of relatives, and these too merely for show. There is a vast swarm of attendants, some for his table and some for his daily needs, whom he drags along as he goes out and comes back, and he is envied by those who meet him. Add to the wealth some political power, or honors from kings, or the governance of nations, or command of armies: the herald shouting loudly before him, the lictors on either side striking blows that fill the governed with the heaviest dread, the confiscations, the arrests, the prisons, from which an unbearable fear is gathered from those under his hand. And what comes after this? One night, or a single fever, or pleurisy, or pneumonia, carries the man off, snatched away from among human beings, and is gone, suddenly stripping bare the whole stage-setting around him, and that glory was confuted like a dream. So the prophet's comparison of human glory to the weakest flower has hit the mark.

"Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, bearing seed according to kind and according to likeness" (Genesis 1:11). Even now the order of growing things testifies to that first arrangement. For sprouting comes first for every herb and every grass. Whether something is sent out from a root by a shoot from below, like the crocus and the dog's-tooth grass, it must first sprout and push out to the surface; or whether it comes from seed, in that case too there must first be sprouting, then the herb, then the green grass, then the fruit ripening on the now dry and thick stalk. "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass." When the seed falls into earth that has a proper measure of moisture and warmth, it becomes porous and full of holes, takes hold of the surrounding earth, and draws to itself the things that are akin and of the same kind. The finest particles of the seed enter the pores of the earth and slip through them, and they widen its own bulk more and more, so that the seed takes root downward and pushes upward, sending out stalks equal in number to the roots. As the sprout is continually warmed, the moisture drawn through the roots brings up with it, by the pull of the heat, a measured amount of the earth's nourishment, and distributes it into stalk and husk and the sheaths of the grain, and into the grain itself and the awns. And so, as the growth proceeds little by little, each of the growing things reaches its proper measure, whether it is one of the grains, or the legumes, or the vegetables, or the brushwood.

One grass and one herb is enough to occupy your whole mind in contemplating the skill that produced them: how the stalk of the grain is girded with joints, so that like some kind of bindings they easily bear the weight of the ears when they are full of fruit and bend down toward the ground. For this reason brome-grass is entirely hollow, since its head is weighed down by nothing; but the grain nature has secured with these bindings. And it has placed the kernel in a sheath so that it is not easily snatched away by seed-pickers; and further, by the projection of the awns, as with points, it keeps off the harm from small creatures.
orientation: Basil is preaching on the creation of vegetation, and has just compared human glory to the flower of grass; he now expands that comparison with a portrait of a powerful man, then turns to the literal process by which seeds sprout and grow.

title: Poisonous plants and the purpose of all creation
english: What shall I say? What shall I pass over in silence? In the rich treasuries of creation, the discovery of the more valuable thing is difficult, and most grievous is the loss of what has been set before us. "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass" (Genesis 1:11). And immediately the poisons were sent out together with the nourishing plants: with the grain, hemlock; with the other foods, hellebore, and aconite, and mandrake, and the juice of the poppy. What then? Shall we abandon giving thanks for the useful things and accuse the Creator for the things that destroy our life? And shall we not reckon this: that not all things have been created for the sake of our stomach? But the foods assigned to us are ready at hand and easily recognized by all; yet each of the things that came into being fulfills its own particular purpose in creation. For since bull's blood is poison to you, was it necessary for this reason either that the bull not be created, or that it be created without blood—whose strength our life needs for so many purposes? But the reason that dwells with you is sufficient for guarding against destructive things. For surely sheep and goats know how to flee from what harms their life, distinguishing what is harmful by sense perception alone; but for you, who have reason at hand, and the medical art supplying what is useful, and the experience of those who came before suggesting flight from harmful things—tell me, is it difficult to avoid poisons? And none of these things has come into being idly, none uselessly. For either it provides food for some of the brute animals, or it has been discovered by the medical art for our own relief from certain illnesses. For starlings feed on hemlock, escaping the harm of the poison through the construction of their bodies. Since they have narrow passages around the heart, they digest what they have swallowed before the chill from it can seize their vital parts. Hellebore is food for quails, which escape the harm by the peculiarity of their constitution. And these very things are also useful to us at times. For through mandrake doctors induce sleep; and with opium they lull the violent pains of the body. Some have already withered the rabid frenzy of appetites with hemlock; and with hellebore they have pried out many chronic afflictions. So what you thought you had as an accusation against the Creator has turned around for you into an increase of thanksgiving.

"Let the earth sprout the herb of grass" (Genesis 1:11). How much spontaneous food he speaks of in these words—the food in roots, and in the herb itself, and already in fruits? And how much that comes to us from care and farming? He did not command seed and fruit to be produced immediately, but the earth to sprout and grow green, and then to be perfected into seed, so that that first command might become a teacher to nature for the sequence that followed. How then, someone says, does the earth bring forth seeds according to kind, when we often sow wheat and harvest this black wheat? But this is not a change to another kind, but a kind of disease and weakness of the seed. For it has not put off being wheat, but has been blackened through scorching, as one can learn from the very name.
orientation: Basil is expounding the command 'Let the earth bring forth the herb of grass' and answering the objection that God created harmful plants.

title: The earth's first vegetation and the seed-bearing trees
english: For when it is burned by excess of cold, it changes to another color and taste. And indeed it is said that when it finds suitable soil and temperate air, it returns to its original form. So you would find nothing among growing things that comes to pass apart from the command. But the so-called darnel, and all the other bastard seeds mixed in with the nourishing ones—which Scripture customarily calls tares—do not come from a change in the wheat, but arise from their own origin, having their own kind. These fill out the image of those who counterfeit the Lord's teachings and are not genuinely discipled by the word, but are corrupted by the teaching of the evil one and mix themselves into the healthy body of the Church, so that from hiding they may inflict their own harms on the more innocent. Already the Lord also likens the perfecting of those who have believed in him to the growth of seeds, saying: "As when a man casts the seed on the ground, and sleeps, and rises night and day, and the seed rises and lengthens, he does not know how. For the earth bears fruit by itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear" (Mark 4:26-28). "Let the earth bring forth vegetation" (Genesis 1:11). And in the briefest moment of time, the earth began from the sprouting, so that it might keep the laws of its Creator, and passing through every form of growth, it immediately brought the sprouts to completion. The meadows were deep with the abundance of grass, and the fruitful plains, bristling with standing crops, preserved the image of a swelling sea in the movement of the ears of grain. Every herb and every kind of vegetable, and whatever belongs to brushwood and whatever belongs to pulses, then abounded on the earth in all abundance. For there was no failure among the things then brought forth: neither the inexperience of farmers, nor the harshness of the air, nor any other cause was harming what came to be. Nor indeed did the condemnation hinder the fertility of the earth. For these things are older than the sin for which we were condemned to eat our bread in the sweat of our face (Genesis 3:19).

But also, he says, "a fruit-bearing tree, producing fruit, whose seed is in it according to kind and according to likeness upon the earth" (Genesis 1:11). At this word all the thickets grew dense; all the trees sprang up—those that by nature rise to the greatest height, firs and cedars, cypresses and pines. All the shrubs were at once leafy on both sides and thick. And the plants called garland-making—the rosebeds and myrtles and laurels—all in one moment of time, not previously existing above the earth, came into being, each with its own proper character, separated by the clearest differences from those of other kinds, and each recognized by its own mark. Except that the rose was then without a thorn; later the thorn was yoked to the beauty of the flower, so that close beside the delight of enjoyment we might have the grief placed nearby, remembering the sin for which the earth was condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles for us (Genesis 3:18). But it was commanded, he says, that the earth put forth "a fruit-bearing tree, producing fruit upon the earth, whose seed is in it." Yet we see many trees that have neither fruit nor seed.
orientation: Basil is explaining the third day of creation, arguing that every plant and tree came forth at God's command with its own seed and kind, not by transformation from one kind into another.

title: Trees without visible fruit still have seed; the vine as image of the soul
english: What shall we say then? That the more valuable things by nature have obtained the first mention; and then, that to one who examines carefully, all things will appear either to use seed or to have what is equivalent to seed. For poplars, and willows, and elms, and white poplars, and all such trees seem to bear no fruit from what is evident, but one who examines carefully would discover that each of these has seed. For the kernel under the leaf, which some of those who have occupied themselves with word-making call 'mischos,' has the power of seed. For whatever naturally comes to be from branches, for the most part puts forth roots from this. And perhaps the offshoots of the roots also hold the place of seed, which the gardeners pull off and increase the kind. But first, as we said, the things more essential to our life were deemed worthy of mention, all that were going to receive man with their own fruits and prepare for him an abundant way of life: the vine producing wine that was going to gladden the heart of man, and the olive providing fruit able to make the face cheerful with oil (Psalm 103:15 (104:15)). How many things came together at the same time, brought forth urgently by nature? The root of the vine; the branches around it, flourishing and great, spread above the ground; the shoot, the tendrils, the unripe grape, the clusters. A vine seen with understanding is enough for your sight to produce in you a reminder of nature. For you remember clearly the image of the Lord, that he calls himself the vine, and the Father the vinedresser, and he called each one of us, having been grafted into the Church through faith, branches (John 15:1-2). And he summons us to abundant fruit, so that we may not be condemned for uselessness and handed over to the fire. And he does not cease everywhere to compare the souls of men to vines. For a vineyard was made for the beloved, he says, on a horn, in a rich place (Isaiah 5:1). And, I planted a vineyard, and put a hedge around it (Isaiah 5:2). He clearly means the human souls as the vineyard, around which he put a hedge—the security from the commandments and the guard of the angels. For the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him (Psalm 33:8 (34:7)). Then he also fixed stakes for us, as it were, placing in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers (1 Corinthians 12:28). And by the examples of the ancient and blessed men he leads our thoughts to the height, and did not leave them thrown on the ground and worthy of being trampled. He also wants us to hold fast to our neighbors by the twining of love, as if by tendrils, and to rest upon them, so that always having our impulse toward what is above, like some climbing vines we may set ourselves beside the tops of the highest things. He also requires us to accept being dug around. And the soul is dug around in the putting away of the cares of the world, which are a weight on our hearts. So the one who has put away fleshly love, and the friendship toward money, or has considered the anxiety for this wretched little glory to be spit upon and contemptible, has been dug around, as it were, and has breathed again, having put off the vain weight of the earthly mind. But it is necessary, according to the word of the proverb, not to grow wild like wood—that is, not to live ostentatiously, nor to hunt for praise from outsiders—but to be fruitful, storing up the display of works for the true vinedresser.
orientation: Basil is answering an objection about Genesis 1:11, that many trees seem to have neither fruit nor seed, and then turns to the vine as a moral image.

title: The olive tree, the variety of plants, and the moral lesson of cultivation
english: And you, be as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, never being stripped of hope, but always keeping the salvation through faith flourishing around you. For in this way you will imitate the evergreen quality of the plant, and you will also rival its abundance of fruit, offering generous almsgiving at every season. But let us return to the investigation of the skilled arrangements. How many kinds of plants sprang up then—some bearing fruit, some for roofing, others suitable for shipbuilding, others for burning? In these again, the arrangement of each tree's parts is varied, and the discovery of each one's particular character is hard to attain, as is the observation of its difference from each of the other kinds. How is it that some of them are deep-rooted and others shallow-rooted, and some grow upright with a single stem, while others are low-growing and immediately divided from the root into many shoots? How is it that those whose branches stretch far out into the air also have deep roots, spreading widely in a circle, as if nature places certain foundations beneath, corresponding to the weight of the things above? How many are the differences of the barks? For some plants are smooth-barked, others cracked-barked; and some of them have a single layer of bark, others many folds. And what is wonderful is that you would find in plants symptoms closely resembling those of human youth and old age. For in the young and flourishing the bark is stretched tight around them, but in those that grow old it becomes wrinkled, as it were, and rough. And some, when cut, sprout again; but others remain without successors, as if enduring the cutting as a kind of death. Indeed, some have observed that pines, when cut down or even burned over, turn into oak forests. And we know that some trees are cured of their natural badness by the care of farmers—for example, the sharp pomegranates and the more bitter almonds, when their trunk near the root is pierced and they receive a greasy wedge of pine driven through the middle of the pith, then change the unpleasantness of their juice into usefulness. Let no one, then, who lives in wickedness despair of himself, knowing that farming changes the qualities of plants, and the care of the soul according to virtue is able to overcome all kinds of infirmities. And the difference in the fruit-bearing of fruit trees is so great that no one could even cover it in speech. For not only are there differences of fruit among the different kinds, but even within the very species of a tree there is much variation; indeed, the growers distinguish one character of fruit for the male trees and another for the female, and they divide even the palms into male and female. And you might at some time see the one they call female letting down her branches, as if in heat, and longing for the embrace of the male; and the tenders of the plants cast into the branches, as it were, certain seeds of the males, the so-called gall-insects, and so she becomes, as it were, aware of the enjoyment, and her branches straighten up again, and her foliage is restored to the proper shape of the plant. They say the same things also about the fig trees.
orientation: Basil is addressing his congregation, drawing moral lessons from the plant world as he continues his exposition of the third day of creation.

title: Wild figs help tame figs; nature's hidden wisdom
english: That is why some growers plant wild fig trees beside the cultivated ones, while others tie wild figs onto the fruitful, tame fig trees and so cure their weakness, using the wild figs to stop the fruit when it is already running off and scattering. What does this riddle from nature mean for you? It means that we must often draw a certain vigor even from those outside the faith, for the display of good works. If you see someone living a pagan life, or cut off from the Church by some crooked heresy, yet practicing a self-controlled life and the rest of good order in conduct, then stretch your own zeal further, so that you may become like the fruit-bearing fig tree, which gathers strength from the presence of the wild figs, stops its running, and nourishes its fruit more carefully. Such, then, are the differences in the manner of their generation, to mention only a very few out of very many. And who could go through the variety of the fruits themselves—their shapes, their colors, the peculiar quality of their juices, the usefulness of each one? How is it that some ripen naked in the sun, while others are filled out covered in husks? And why is the covering of the leaf thick for those whose fruit is soft, as with the fig tree, while for those whose fruits are more tightly enclosed, the growth of leaves is light, as with the walnut tree? Because the former, being weak, needed more help, while for the latter a thicker covering would have been harmful because of the shade it cast. How is the leaf of the vine split apart, so that the grape cluster can withstand the harms that come from the air, and yet receive the sun's ray generously through the open spaces? Nothing is without cause; nothing happens by chance; everything contains some inexpressible wisdom. What words could reach it? How could the human mind go through everything with precision, so as to observe the peculiarities, clearly distinguish the differences in each case, and set forth the hidden causes without omission? One and the same water is drawn up through the root, yet it nourishes the root itself in one way, the bark of the stem in another, the wood in another, and the pith in yet another. The same water becomes leaf, and is divided out into shoots and branches, and supplies growth to the fruits, and from the same source comes the tear of the plant and its resinous juice—and no words could reach how great the difference among these is. For the tear of the mastic tree is one thing, and the sap of the balsam is another; and certain giant fennel plants in Egypt and Libya weep out another kind of sap. There is also a story that amber is the sap of plants, hardened into the nature of stone. The bits of wood and the tiniest creatures that appear inside it bear witness to this story, since they were caught and held while the sap was still soft. In general, someone who has not been taught by experience will find no account that can set forth the activity behind the differences in the qualities of these saps. Again, how is it that from the same moisture wine is formed in the vine, and oil in the olive? And this is not the only wonder—how the liquid is sweetened here and becomes oily there—but also that among the sweet fruits there is an indescribable variation of quality.
orientation: Basil is still expounding the vegetation of the third day, drawing moral and theological lessons from the way plants grow and bear fruit.

title: One water, many tastes and colors in plants
english: For the sweet quality in the vine is one thing, and that in the apple tree, the fig, and the date palm is another. I want you to linger with me over this inquiry a little longer: how the same water is smooth to the senses at one moment, when it becomes sweetened in certain plants, and at another moment it is striking to the taste, when it is made sour as it passes through other plants. And again, when it changes into extreme bitterness, it roughens the sense, as happens in wormwood or scammony. In acorns, or the fruit of the cornel tree, it changes into an astringent and harsh quality; but in terebinths and walnut trees, it is transformed into a soft and oily nature.

And why speak of distant examples, when in the same fig tree it passes over into the most opposite qualities? For it is most bitter in the sap, but most sweet in the fruit itself. And on the vine it is most astringent in the shoots, but most pleasant in the grape clusters. And how many are the differences in colors? You could see in a meadow the same water reddened in one flower, and in another purple, and dark blue in this one, and white in another; and again it provides a difference in scents that is even greater than the variety in colors.

But I see that my discourse is falling into excess through the insatiability of contemplation. Unless I bind it and lead it back to the necessity of the creation account, the day will fail me while I am presenting to you the great wisdom from the smallest things. “Let the earth sprout a fruit-bearing tree, producing fruit upon the earth” (Genesis 1:11). And immediately the mountain peaks were covered with foliage, and gardens were artfully arranged, and riverbanks were adorned with countless kinds of plants. Some had been prepared to adorn the human table; others were providing food for the herds, from their leaves and from their fruits. Others were furnishing us in advance with the benefits of medicine: their juices, their saps, their twigs, their barks, their fruit. And in a word, all the useful things that long experience has discovered for us, gathering what is beneficial from particular occurrences—these the keen forethought of the Creator, foreseeing them from the beginning, brought into being.

But you, whenever you see the cultivated plants, the wild ones, those that love water, those that grow on dry land, those that bear flowers, or those without flowers—recognizing the great in the small—always add to your wonder, and increase for me your love of the Creator. Examine how he made some plants evergreen, and others that are stripped bare; and among the evergreen ones, some shed their leaves, while others are ever-leafed. For both the olive and the pine shed their leaves, even if they exchange their foliage imperceptibly, so that they never seem to be stripped of their covering. But the date palm is ever-leafed, keeping the same leaf from its first sprouting to the end. Then consider also this: how the tamarisk is like an amphibious creature, numbered among the plants that love water, and yet multiplying in the deserts. For this reason Jeremiah fittingly compares the more wicked and wavering characters to this plant.
“Let the earth sprout” (Genesis 1:11). This small command was immediately a great nature and an artful principle, completing the countless properties of growing things more swiftly than our thought.
orientation: Basil is expounding the third day of creation, showing how the same water produces different qualities in different plants, and then turns to the command 'Let the earth bring forth' as the source of all plant life.

title: The command still drives the earth, and the hearer must come prepared
english: That command still even now existing in the earth urges it on, in each yearly cycle, to bring out all the power it has for the generation of plants, seeds, and trees. For just as tops, once the first blow is given them, make their subsequent rotations when they fix their point in themselves and spin around, so too the sequence of nature, having received its beginning from the first command, passes through all the time that follows, until it arrives at the common completion of the universe. Toward that completion may we all press on, fruitful and full of good works, so that, planted in the house of the Lord, we may bloom in the courts of our God, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
Homily 6: On the creation of the lights.

A spectator of athletes ought to share in some measure of their vigor. One can see this from the rules of the festivals, which prescribe that those sitting together in the stadium sit with bare heads—in my opinion, so that each person may be not only a spectator of the contestants but also in his own turn a contestant. So too, then, the examiner of great and extraordinary spectacles, and the hearer of truly supreme and ineffable wisdom, ought to come with some resources of his own for the contemplation of what lies before us, and to share in my struggle as far as he is able—standing by not so much as a judge as a fellow contestant. Otherwise the discovery of the truth may escape us, and my error may become a common loss for the hearers.

Why do I say this? Because since our task is the examination of the world's constitution and the contemplation of the universe—a task whose principles come not from the wisdom of the world, but from what God taught his servant, speaking to him plainly and not through riddles—it is altogether necessary that those who love to behold great things not have an untrained mind for the understanding of what lies before us. If ever, then, on a clear night you have gazed at the ineffable beauties of the stars and received a thought of the craftsman of all things—who it is who has adorned the heaven with these flowers, and how in visible things the necessary exceeds the delightful—and again by day, if with sober reasoning you have studied the wonders of the day and through visible things have inferred the invisible one, you have come as a prepared hearer, fit for the fullness of this solemn and blessed theater.

Come then—just as those who take strangers by the hand and lead them around a city—so I myself will guide you through the hidden wonders of this great city. In this city is our ancient homeland, from which the man-slaying demon removed us, having enslaved man by his own enticements. Here you will see the first origin of man, and the death that immediately overtook us—death, which sin bore, the firstborn offspring of the evil-originating demon. And you will come to know yourself: earthly in nature, yet the work of divine hands; in power far inferior to the irrational animals, yet appointed ruler by election of the irrational and the lifeless.
orientation: Basil is closing his homily on the third day's vegetation and opening the sixth homily, on the creation of the lights, by urging his hearers to come as fellow contestants, not mere judges.

title: Man lifted toward heaven and the lights of the fourth day
english: By nature he falls short of the animals in bodily gifts, yet by abundance of reason he can be lifted toward heaven. If we learn this, we shall know ourselves fully, we shall know God, we shall worship our Creator, we shall serve the Master, we shall glorify the Father, we shall love our nourisher, we shall revere our benefactor, and we shall never cease worshipping the author of our present life and the life to come, who confirms His promises by the riches He has already given and makes our hopes secure by the proof of present blessings.

If passing things are so rich, what must eternal things be like? If visible things are so beautiful, what must invisible things be like? If the vastness of heaven surpasses the measure of human thought, what mind could trace out the nature of eternal things?

The sun is subject to decay, yet it is so beautiful and so great, swift in movement and returning in well-ordered circuits, with a size fitted to the whole so that it keeps proportion to the universe, and by natural beauty shining upon creation like a bright eye. If gazing at it never wearies us, how beautiful must the sun of righteousness be? If it is a loss for a blind man not to see this sun, how great a loss is it for a sinner to be cut off from the true light?

Heaven and earth already existed. Light had been made over them. Day and night had been divided. Then came the firmament once more, and the revealing of dry land. The water had been gathered into one settled and separate gathering. The earth was full of its own offspring, sprouting countless kinds of plants and rich with every sort of plant. Yet sun and moon did not yet exist, so that those who do not know God would neither name the sun the first source and father of light nor reckon it the maker of what grows from the earth. For this reason the fourth day came, and then, Basil says, God said, "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven for shining upon the earth, to divide between day and between night" (Genesis 1:14).

When you are taught who spoke, join the hearer to Him at once in thought. For Scripture says God said, "Let there be lights," and then that God made the two lights (Genesis 1:16). Who spoke and who made? Basil asks you to see in this doubling the two persons. Throughout the history the teaching about God is sown like seed in mystery. The purpose for the birth of the lights is also added: for shining, Scripture says, upon the earth. If light had already come to be, how is the sun now said to have come to be again for shining? First, Basil says, let no strangeness in the wording move you to laughter. We do not follow your fine choice of words, nor do we chase neat rhythm in placing them. We are no polishers of phrases. Everywhere we prize clear meaning in words above sweet sound. See whether by shining he showed well enough what he wished, for he said shining instead of illumination. This quarrels in nothing with what was said about light. Then the very nature of light was brought forth, while now this body of the sun has been prepared as a vehicle for that first-born light.
orientation: Basil finishes urging his hearers to know themselves and then starts explaining the fourth day of creation.

title: Light and its vehicle are distinct
english: For just as fire is one thing and a lamp another—the one possessing the power to give light, the other made to shine for those who need it—so also the lights were now prepared as a vehicle for that purest and unmixed and immaterial light. For as the apostle says, there are certain lights in the world (Philippians 2:15), but the true light of the world is something else (John 1:9), and by sharing in it the saints became lights for the souls they taught, rescuing them from the darkness of ignorance. In the same way, the Maker of all things fitted this sun to that most radiant light and kindled it around the world.

And let no one think what has been said is unbelievable—that the brightness of light is one thing, and the body underlying the light is another. First, then, from the fact that all composite things are divided by us in this way, into the receptive substance and the quality that has come upon it. Just as whiteness is one thing by nature and the whitened body another, so also the things now spoken of, being different by nature, have been united by the power of the Creator. And do not tell me that it is impossible for these to be divided from one another. For I do not claim that the division of light from the solar body is possible for you and me, but that what is separable for us in thought can also be separated in actual operation by the Maker of their nature. Since even for you it is impossible to separate the burning power of fire from its brightness; yet God, wishing to turn his servant by a marvelous sight, placed fire on the bush that was active from its brightness alone, while its power to burn remained idle (Exodus 3:2). As the psalmist also testifies when he says, “The voice of the Lord divides the flame of fire” (Psalm 28:7 LXX). From this also, in the repayment of the lives we have lived, a certain teaching instructs us in mystery: that the nature of fire will be divided, and the light will be assigned for the enjoyment of the righteous, while the painful part of burning will be appointed for those being punished.

Then, moreover, from the phenomena concerning the moon, it is possible for us to find faith in what we are seeking. For when it wanes and decreases, it is not consumed in its whole body, but by putting off the light that surrounds it and taking it on again, it presents to us the appearances of decrease and increase. And that its body itself is not consumed when it wanes has clear testimony in what is seen. For you can, in clear air free from all mist, especially when it happens to be crescent-shaped, observe and see its unlit and unilluminated part outlined by an arc as large as the one that fills the whole of it at full moon. So the completed circle is clearly seen, with the eye bringing together the shadowy and misty hollow with the illuminated part. And do not tell me that the moon's light is imported, because it decreases as it moves toward the sun and increases again as it draws away. For that is not what we are examining at present, but rather that its body is one thing, and what gives it light is another.
orientation: Basil is explaining the fourth day of creation, arguing that the sun and moon are not the light itself but vehicles prepared for the first-created light.

title: Sun and moon as signs and the nature of night
english: Think of the sun in the same way, with one difference: the sun received the light once and holds it blended with itself, and never puts it off. The moon, by contrast, is continually stripping off the light, so to speak, and putting it on again, and by its own behavior it confirms what has been said about the sun. These lights were also appointed to separate between the day and between the night. For above, God separated between the light and between the darkness; then he set their natures in opposition to each other, so that they have no mixing with one another, and light has nothing in common with darkness. What a shadow is in the daytime, that is what we should understand the nature of darkness to be at night. For every shadow falls from bodies that block a shining ray, lying opposite the light; in the morning it stretches toward the west, in the evening it leans toward the east, and at noon it lies to the north. So too the night withdraws in the direction opposite the sun's rays, being nothing other in its nature than a shadowing of the earth. Just as in the daytime a shadow comes into being from whatever blocks the light, so the night naturally comes into being when the air around the earth is cast into shadow. This, then, is what is meant by the words, God separated between the light and between the darkness: the darkness flees the assaults of the light, because at the first creation their estrangement from one another was built into their natures. But now he commanded the sun to govern the measures of the day, and the moon, whenever it completes its own cycle, he made the ruler of the night. For at that time the lights stand nearly opposite one another across the diameter. When the sun rises at the full moon, the moon sinks down out of sight; and when the sun sets again, the moon often rises opposite it from the east. If in its other phases the moon's light does not exactly coincide with the night, that has no bearing on the present discussion. The point is that when the moon is at its fullest, it begins the night, outshining the stars with its own light and illuminating the earth, and it divides the measures of time equally with the sun. "And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years" (Genesis 1:14). The indications given by the lights are necessary for human life. If one does not busy himself beyond measure with the signs they give, he will find their observations, gained from long experience, useful. From them one can learn many things about heavy rain, and many things about droughts and the movement of winds, whether local or general, violent or gentle. One of the signs drawn from the sun the Lord himself has handed on to us, when he said, "There will be a storm, for the sky reddens, being gloomy" (Matthew 16:3). For when the sun rises through mist, its rays are dimmed, and its color appears like coals and tinged with blood, because the thickness of the air produces this appearance to the eyes. The air, which until then was dense and compact and not dispersed by the ray, shows that it could not be overcome because of the influx of vapors from the earth, but by the excess of moisture it will bring a storm upon the regions where it gathers.
orientation: Basil is explaining the fourth day's creation of the sun and moon, arguing that night is simply the earth's shadow and that the lights were appointed to mark times and give signs for human life.

title: Weather signs and the refutation of astrology
english: In the same way, when the moon is surrounded by a halo, and when the so-called halos form around the sun, they indicate either an abundance of moisture in the air or the onset of violent winds. And when what they call counter-suns accompany the sun's course, these too become signs of certain disturbances in the air. So also the rods that appear upright in the clouds with the color of a rainbow point to rain or extraordinary storms, or in general indicate above all a change in the atmosphere. Those who have devoted themselves to these matters have also observed many signs connected with the moon's waxing and waning, since the air around the earth necessarily changes along with the moon's phases. For when the moon is thin and clear on about the third day, it promises settled fair weather; but when it appears thick, with reddish horns, it threatens either violent rain from the clouds or a forceful south wind. Who does not know how much benefit these signs bring to daily life? A sailor can keep his vessel inside the harbor when he foresees the dangers from the winds. A traveler can avoid harm from afar by waiting out the change signaled by the gloominess of the air. And farmers, who labor over seeds and the care of plants, find from these signs all the right times for their work.
