The Lord has also foretold that signs of the dissolution of the universe will appear in the sun and the moon and the stars: "The sun will be turned to blood, and the moon will not give its light" (Joel 2:31; cf. Acts 2:20). These are signs of the completion of all things.

But those who leap beyond the bounds drag the discussion to the defense of astrology, and they say that our life is bound to the movement of the heavenly bodies, and that this is why the Chaldeans derive from the stars their predictions of what happens to us. They take the simple statement of Scripture, "Let them be for signs," and twist it to their own liking, as if it referred not to changes in the air or the seasons but to the allotment of human lives. For what do they say? They say that the interweaving of certain moving stars with the stars positioned in the zodiac, when they come together in a particular configuration, produces certain births; and that a different relation of these same stars produces the opposite allotment of life. About these matters it is perhaps not useless, for the sake of clarity, to go back a little and speak. I will say nothing of my own invention, but I will use their own arguments against them for their refutation—offering a kind of healing to those already caught in the harm, and security to the rest so that they do not fall into the same errors. The inventors of this astrology, having observed that in the broad span of time many of the configurations escaped them, confined the measures of time to an extremely narrow point. They claim that even the very smallest and most instantaneous moment—what the apostle calls "in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye" (1 Corinthians 15:52)—makes the greatest difference between one birth and another. The one born in this instant, they say, will be a tyrant over cities and a ruler of peoples, exceedingly wealthy and powerful; while the one born in the other moment of time will be a beggar and a vagabond, going from door to door for his daily food.
orientation: Basil is explaining the usefulness of the heavenly lights as signs for weather and seasons, then begins refuting those who misuse them for astrology.

title: Astrology's absurd precision and its animal logic
english: For this reason they divided the circle called the zodiac into twelve parts, and because the sun passes through one twelfth of the sphere called the fixed sphere in thirty days, they divided each of the twelfth-parts into thirty degrees. Then they divided each degree into sixty parts, and each of those sixtieths they cut again sixty times. So when they set down the births of children, let us see whether they can preserve this precision in dividing time. For the child is born, and at the same moment the midwife examines whether the newborn is male or female; then she waits for the cry, which is the sign that the child is alive. How many sixtieths do you suppose pass by in that time? Then she tells the Chaldean that the child has been born. Through how many of the very finest divisions, do you suppose, the midwife's voice travels—especially if the one who is supposed to fix the hour happens to be standing outside the women's quarters? For the one who intends to study horoscopes must record the hour with precision, whether it is by day or by night. What a swarm of sixtieths passes by again in that time! For it is necessary, they say, to determine not only in which twelfth-part the star that marks the hour is, but also in which degree of that twelfth-part, and in which sixtieth—into which we said the degree is divided—or, to find the exact point, in which sixtieth of the subdivisions of the first sixtieths. And they say it is necessary to make this extremely fine and incomprehensible determination of time for each of the planets, so as to find what relation they had to the fixed stars, and what configuration they had toward one another at the moment of the child's birth. So if it is impossible to hit upon the hour exactly, and the variation of the very briefest moment causes one to miss everything, then both those who have devoted themselves to this non-existent art are ridiculous, and so are those who gape at them as though they could know what concerns them. 6.6 And what are the results like? 'So-and-so,' he says, 'is curly-haired and bright-eyed, for he has the Ram as his ascendant; for the animal is seen somewhat like that.' But he is also high-minded, because the Ram is a leader; and open-handed, and again resourceful, because this animal both sheds its wool without pain and is easily clothed again by nature. 'But the one born under the Bull,' he says, 'is hardy and servile, because the bull is under the yoke.' And the one born under the Scorpion is a striker, because of his likeness to the beast. The one born under the Scales is just, because of the equality of scales among us. What could be more ridiculous than these things? The Ram, from which you take the birth of a human being, is a twelfth part of heaven, in which the sun comes to touch the signs of spring. And the Scales and the Bull likewise—each of these is a twelfth-part of the circle called the zodiac. How then, when you say that the primary causes for human lives exist, do you characterize the characters of people born from our domestic animals? For the one born under the Ram is open-handed, not because that part of heaven produces such a character, but because the sheep has such a nature. Why then do you try to overawe us with the authority of the stars, while attempting to persuade us through bleatings? For if heaven received such peculiarities of character from the animals, then heaven itself is subject to alien principles, having its causes derived from cattle. But if it is ridiculous to say this, it is far more ridiculous to try to bring into the argument plausibilities drawn from things that have nothing in common with it.
orientation: Basil is refuting astrology by showing that its own demand for exact birth-times is impossible, and then mocking its use of zodiac animals to explain human character.

title: Astrology's webs and the absurdity of fate
english: But these clever arguments of theirs are like spider webs: when a gnat or a fly or some other weak creature of that kind gets caught in them, it is held fast; but when one of the stronger animals comes near, it slips through easily and tears the flimsy webs apart and destroys them.

And they do not stop at these things alone. Even the things over which each of us has authority by our own choice—I mean the pursuits of virtue or vice—even these they connect to causes in the heavens. To argue against them in any other way would be laughable, but because so many people are already held captive by the deception, it is perhaps necessary not to pass over it in silence.

First, then, let us ask them this: do not the configurations of the stars change countless times every day? For the so-called planets are always in motion, and some overtake one another more quickly, while others make their circuits more slowly, and at the same hour they often both see one another and are hidden from one another. And the greatest power in nativities, as they themselves say, lies in whether a person is watched over by a beneficent star or a maleficent one. And often, when they fail to discover the exact moment at which the beneficent star was bearing witness, because of ignorance of one of the smallest details, they record the person as lying under evil fortune. For I am compelled to use their own words.

In such arguments there is much foolishness, and far more impiety. For the maleficent stars transfer the cause of their own wickedness to the one who made them. If their evil comes from their nature, then the Creator will be the maker of evil. But if they become evil by choice, then first of all they will be creatures with choice, using free and self-governing impulses—which is beyond madness to attribute falsely to soulless things. And then how irrational it is: evil and good are not distributed to each according to merit, but because a star happens to be in a certain place, it is beneficent, and because it is seen by another star, the same one becomes maleficent; and again, when it shifts a little from its configuration, it immediately forgets its wickedness.

But let this be enough on those points. If at every indivisible moment of time the stars are rearranged into one configuration after another, and in these countless changes, many times a day, the configurations that produce royal nativities are completed, why are kings not born every day? Or why do they have hereditary successions of kingdoms at all? For surely each king does not carefully arrange the birth of his own son to fit the royal configuration of the stars. What human being has control over such a thing? How then did Uzziah beget Jotham, Jotham Ahaz, Ahaz Hezekiah? And in none of these did anyone happen upon a servile hour of birth?

Furthermore, if the origins of our actions in vice and virtue are not within our power, but the necessities come from our nativity, then lawmakers are superfluous, defining what we should do and what we should avoid; and judges are superfluous too, honoring virtue and punishing wickedness. For the theft is not the thief's fault, nor the murder the murderer's—since it was not possible for him, even if he wanted to, to control his hand, because of the inescapable necessity driving him to the deed.
orientation: Basil is refuting astrology, having just shown that the zodiac signs' supposed characters are borrowed from animals; now he turns to the astrologers' claims about the stars governing human choices and actions.

title: The seasons follow the ordered motion of the lights
english: But the most foolish of all are those who labor at the crafts. The farmer will prosper, they say, without sowing seed or sharpening a sickle, and the merchant will become exceedingly rich whether he wants to or not, because fate gathers wealth for him. Our great Christian hopes will vanish into nothing, since righteousness is not honored and sin is not condemned, because nothing is accomplished by human choice. For where necessity and fate rule, there is no place for what is deserved, which is the special mark of just judgment. So much for those people. You do not need more words from me, since you are sound in your own thinking, and the time does not allow me to stretch out my response to them beyond measure.

Let us return to the next words of the text. "Let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years," it says (Genesis 1:14). We have already spoken about the signs. By seasons, I think he means the alternations of the year's periods: winter, spring, summer, and autumn. The ordered movement of the lights causes us to pass through these in good order. Winter comes when the sun lingers in the southern regions and produces a long stretch of nighttime shadow over our part of the earth, so that the air around the earth grows cold, and all the moist vapors gather around us and bring about rain, frost, and boundless snow. But when the sun returns again from the southern regions and reaches the midpoint, so that it divides the time equally between night and day, the more it lingers over the places above the earth, the more it gradually brings back a mild temperature. Then spring comes, which is the beginning of sprouting for all plants, grants renewal of life to most trees, and preserves the race of all land and water creatures through the succession of their offspring. From there the sun drives on toward the summer solstice, toward the Bear itself, and brings about the longest days for us. Because it stays in contact with the air for the greatest length of time, it scorches the air above our heads and dries out the whole earth, and in this way it helps the seeds to mature and urges the fruits of the trees toward ripeness. At that time the sun is at its most blazing, making the shadows short at midday, because it shines down on our region from on high. The longest days are those in which the shadows are shortest, and the shortest days are those in which the shadows are longest. This is true for us who are called different-shadowed, all of us who inhabit the northern parts of the earth. For there are already some people who, for two days of the whole year, become completely shadowless at midday. The sun shines down on them from directly overhead and illuminates them equally from every side, so that even the water in deep wells is lit up through their narrow openings. That is why some call them shadowless. But those beyond the spice-bearing land cast their shadows alternately to both sides. They are the only ones in our inhabited world who send their shadows toward the south at midday. That is why some have named them double-shadowed.
orientation: Basil is expounding Genesis 1:14, explaining that the lights serve 'for seasons' by governing the orderly cycle of winter, spring, summer, and autumn.

title: The sun's course and the greatness of the lights
english: All these things happen when the sun has already passed by toward the northern region. From these facts one can infer how great the burning is that the sun's ray produces in the air, and what kinds of effects it brings about. Then the season of autumn receives us, and it breaks down the excess of the stifling heat. Little by little it lets up on the warmth, and through the moderate mean of its mixture it leads us unharmed through itself into winter—clearly because the sun is turning back again from the northern regions toward the south. These turnings of the seasons, which follow the movements of the sun, order our life for us.

But let them be, Scripture says, also for days—not so as to make days, but so as to rule over the days. For day and night are older than the creation of the lights. The psalm shows us this when it says: He set the sun for authority over the day, the moon and stars for authority over the night (Psalm 135:8-9 LXX; Hebrew 136:8-9). How then does the sun have authority over the day? Because it carries light in itself, and whenever it rises above our horizon, it provides day by dissolving the darkness. So no one would go wrong in defining day as the air illuminated by the sun, or in defining day as a measure of time in which the sun spends its course in the hemisphere above the earth.

But the sun and moon were also appointed for years. The moon, whenever it completes its own course twelve times, produces a year—except that it often needs an intercalary month for the exact convergence of the seasons, as the Hebrews of old reckoned the year, and the most ancient of the Greeks. A solar year is the return of the sun by its own movement from the same point back to the same point.

And God made the two great lights. Since the word great in one sense has an absolute meaning—as in great is the heaven, and great is the earth, and great is the sea—but in most cases it naturally refers to something else—as in great is the horse, and the ox is great, for such things receive their testimony of greatness not in the excess of their bodily bulk but in comparison with things like themselves—how then shall we understand the meaning of great? Is it as when we call the ant or some other naturally small thing great, testifying to its superiority by comparison with things of the same kind? Or is great used here in such a way that the greatness is displayed in the very construction of the lights themselves? I think the latter. For they are not great because they are larger than the smaller stars, but because their circumference is so vast that the radiance poured out from them is sufficient to illuminate both heaven and the air, and at the same time to extend over all the earth and the sea. Since they appear in every part of the heaven, rising and setting and holding the middle, they show themselves equal to human beings from every direction. This is clear proof of the abundance of their greatness: the breadth of the earth causes no variation in them so that they seem larger or smaller.
orientation: Basil is explaining the fourth day's creation of the sun and moon, arguing that their size is absolute, not merely relative to smaller stars.

title: The sun's apparent size and true greatness
english: For things that stand far off we see as somehow smaller, and the closer we draw to them, the more we discover their true size. But with the sun, no one is closer and no one farther away; it strikes those settled in every part of the earth from an equal distance. A proof of this is that both Indians and Britons see it the same. For it does not diminish in size as it sets for those who live in the east, nor does it appear smaller as it rises for those settled toward the west; and when it is at mid-heaven, it does not differ from the view on either side. Do not let the appearance deceive you, and do not reckon that because it seems a cubit long to those who see it, it is actually that size. For the sizes of visible things naturally contract at great distances, since the power of sight cannot cross the intervening space, but is, as it were, used up in the middle, and only a small part of it reaches the visible objects. So our sight becomes small, and it makes the things seen be thought small, imposing its own condition on what is visible. Therefore sight lies, and its judgment is untrustworthy. But recall your own experiences, and you will have from yourself the proof of what I am saying. If you have ever seen from a high mountain peak a plain that is broad and level, how large did the teams of oxen appear to you? How big were the plowmen themselves? Did they not give you the impression of ants? And if from a lookout turned toward the open sea you cast your eyes upon the water, how large did the greatest of the islands seem to you? How big did one of the ten-thousand-burden cargo ships appear, carried over the dark blue sea with white sails? Did it not present an impression smaller than any dove? Because, as I said, sight is used up in the air, becomes faint, and is not sufficient for an accurate grasp of what is seen. And indeed, the greatest mountains, cut through with deep ravines, sight declares to be round and smooth, because it reaches only the projections and through weakness cannot enter the hollows between. So it does not even preserve the shapes of bodies as they are, but thinks square towers are round. Thus it is clear from every side that at the greatest distances sight receives not a distinct but a confused impression of bodies. Great, then, is the light, according to the testimony of Scripture, and infinitely greater than what appears.

And let this also be a clear sign to you of its size. Though the stars in heaven are countless in number, the light gathered from them is not enough to dissolve the gloom of night. But this one alone, appearing above the horizon—or rather, even while still expected, before it has fully risen over the earth—makes the darkness vanish, outshines the stars, and melts and disperses the air around the earth that had been fixed and packed together. From this come the morning winds and the dews that flow over the earth in clear weather. And how could it illuminate the whole earth, vast as it is, in a single moment of time, unless it cast its radiance from a great circle? Here learn the wisdom of the craftsman: how he gave it heat proportionate to this distance.
orientation: Basil is explaining why the sun's apparent smallness to human eyes does not disprove its true vastness, arguing from the limits of sight over great distances.

title: The moon's changing shapes teach human mutability
english: Its fiery quality is so measured that it neither burns up the earth through excess nor leaves it frozen and barren through deficiency. And what has been said about the sun should be understood as applying in kind to the moon as well. For its body is also great, and it is the brightest light after the sun. Yet its size does not remain always visible. At one time it appears completed in its circle, at another lacking and diminished, showing its missing part on one side or another. For as it waxes, one part of it is shadowed, and at the time of its waning another part is hidden. There is some inexpressible design of the wise craftsman in this varied alternation of shapes. It is as though he were giving us a clear example of our own nature: that nothing human is stable, but some things proceed from non-being into perfection, while others, after reaching their proper prime and growing to their fullest measure, waste away and perish again through gradual subtractions, and as they diminish they are brought low. So from the sight of the moon we are taught about our own condition, and by taking thought of the swift turning of human affairs we learn not to think highly of life's successes, not to exult in positions of power, not to be lifted up by the uncertainty of wealth, to despise the flesh around which change revolves, and to care for the soul whose good is unshaken. If the moon troubles you as it gradually consumes its light through subtractions, let a soul trouble you more—a soul that has acquired virtue and then through carelessness destroys what is good, never remaining in the same disposition but constantly turning and shifting because of the instability of its purpose. For truly, as it is said, "The fool changes like the moon" (Sirach 27:11). I think too that the change of the moon contributes no small benefit to the constitution of living creatures and to the other things that grow from the earth. Bodies are disposed differently when the moon wanes and when it waxes: when it is declining they become porous and empty, and when it is waxing and hastening toward fullness they are filled up again, because the moon secretly sends down a certain moisture mixed with warmth that reaches into the depths. Those who sleep under the moon show this, as the spaces of their heads are filled with excess moisture; so do freshly slaughtered meats, which quickly turn at the touch of the moon, and the brains of animals, and the moistest parts of sea creatures, and the piths of trees. All these things the moon could not have power to change along with its own alteration unless it were something extraordinary and surpassing in power, according to the testimony of Scripture. And the conditions of the air are also affected along with the moon's changes, as the sudden disturbances at the new moon bear witness to us—when calm and stillness often give way to turmoil, clouds shaken and colliding with one another—and the backflows in the straits, and the ebb tide around what is called the ocean, which those who live nearby have discovered follows the cycles of the moon in an orderly way. For the straits flow back and forth in either direction according to the remaining phases of the moon, but at the time of its birth they do not remain still even for the briefest moment; they are in constant surge and swaying until the moon appears again and gives a certain regularity to the backflow.
orientation: Basil is explaining the fourth day's creation of the sun and moon, and has just described the sun's heat; he now turns to the moon's changing phases and their moral and physical effects.

title: The moon's size and the limits of human reasoning
english: The western sea, by contrast, undergoes its ebb tides, now receding and then flooding over again, as if drawn backward by the moon's exhalations and then pushed forward to its proper measure by her out-breathings. I have said these things to demonstrate the size of the lights and to establish that not even a syllable of the God-inspired words is idle. And yet my discourse has touched on almost none of the essential points. For those who have examined the workings and powers of the sun and moon with care can discover by reasoning a great deal about their sizes and distances. We ought, then, to accuse ourselves honestly of our own weakness, so that the greatest of created works are not measured by our own speech, but rather so that from the few things said we may reckon for ourselves how many and how great are the things left unmentioned.

Do not, therefore, measure even the moon with your eye, but with reasoning, which is far more accurate than the eyes for discovering truth. Some laughable myths, babbled everywhere by old women in their cups, have spread the claim that the moon is moved from her own seat by certain sorceries and brought down to the earth. How could a magician's incantation move her whom the Most High himself established? And what place could receive her if she were dragged down? Do you want to grasp the proof of her size from small indications? The cities throughout the inhabited world, though separated from one another by the greatest distances, all receive the moon's light equally in their streets turned toward the east. If she were not directly opposite them all, she would certainly illuminate those in the straight line of the narrow streets, but for those beyond her breadth she would cast her rays obliquely, slanting them to the sides. This is what one can see happening with lamps in houses. When several people stand around a lamp, the shadow of the one standing directly in front of it extends upright, while the remaining shadows incline to each side. So if the moon's body were not immense and surpassing in size, it would not extend equally opposite to all.

For when she rises from the equatorial regions, those who dwell in the frozen zone and lie beneath the turnings of the Bear receive her light just as those who live in the hollows of the south, neighbors of the scorched zone. Extending opposite to all of them across her breadth, she provides the clearest testimony of her size. Who, then, will deny that her body is enormous, matching such great and numerous distances at once? Let this suffice concerning the sizes of the sun and moon.

May he who granted us understanding to learn the great wisdom of the Craftsman from the smallest things of creation also grant us to receive from the great things even greater conceptions of the Creator. And yet, in comparison with the Maker, the sun and moon hold the rank of a gnat and an ant. For it is not possible to gain from these a vision worthy of the greatness of the God of all things, but only to be led forward by small and faint impressions through them, just as through each of the smallest things among animals or plants.

Let us be content with what has been said. I give thanks to him who granted me this small ministry of the word, and you to him who nourishes you with spiritual food—who even now has fed you, as with some barley bread, through the humble quality of our voice. And may he nourish you forever, granting you the manifestation of the Spirit according to the measure of your faith, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever.
orientation: Basil is concluding his discussion of the fourth day's lights, arguing that the moon's vast size is proven by its simultaneous visibility across distant cities, and that even the greatest heavenly bodies are small compared to God.

title: The waters bring forth living creatures
english: Amen. Homily 7: On Creeping Things. “And God said, ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying across the firmament of heaven according to kind’” (Genesis 1:20). After the creation of the lights, the waters are now filled with living things, so that this region too may be adorned. The earth had already received its adornment from its own plants; the heaven had received the flowers of the stars, and had been adorned as it were by the twin beams of the great lights, like a pair of eyes. What remained was for the waters to receive their own adornment as well. The command came, and at once rivers became active and lakes productive, each of them bringing forth their own natural kinds. The sea gave birth to all the varied kinds of swimming creatures, and not even what was in the mud and pools of water—not even this remained idle or without its share in the work of creation. For frogs and gnats and mosquitoes were clearly produced from them. The things we still see now are proof of what happened then. So every water hastened to serve the creative command; and the great and ineffable power of God showed at once the life of creatures whose kinds no one could even count, active and moving, the moment the command was given and the waters received their fitness for producing life. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls.” Now for the first time a living creature is made that has a soul and shares in sensation. For plants and trees, even if they are said to live because they share in the power of nourishment and growth, are not animals, nor do they have souls. For this reason: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” Everything that swims—whether it floats on the surface of the water or cuts through the depths—belongs to the nature of creeping things, since it moves along through the body of the water. And even if some water creatures have feet and walk (most of these are amphibious—for example, seals, crocodiles, river horses, frogs, and crabs), their primary characteristic is still swimming. For this reason: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” In these few words, what kind has been left out? What has not been included in the command of creation? Are not the live-bearing creatures included—seals, dolphins, torpedo rays, and the similar ones called cartilaginous fish? Are not the egg-laying ones, which are nearly all the kinds of fish? Are not all the scaly ones, all those with rough skins, all those with fins and those without? The sound of the command is small—or rather, it is not even a sound, but only an inclination and impulse of the will. Yet the meaning contained in the command is as vast as all the differences and common features of fish. To go through all of them in detail would be like counting the waves of the sea, or trying to measure the water of the ocean with cups. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” In these are included the creatures of the open sea, the creatures of the shores, the creatures of the depths, the creatures of the rocks, those that move in schools, those that scatter, the sea-monsters, the enormous ones, and the smallest of fish. For by the same power and the same command, both the great and the small receive their existence.
orientation: Basil has finished the fourth day's lights and now expounds the fifth day's command, when God fills the waters with living creatures.

title: Fish belong to the water by nature
english: "Let the waters bring forth." This shows you the natural kinship of swimming creatures with water, which is why fish perish when separated from water even for a short time. They do not have breathing to draw in this air; rather, what air is to land animals, water is to the swimming kind. And the reason is clear. In us, the lung lies within—a porous organ with many passages—which receives air through the expansion of the chest and fans and cools our inner heat. But in them, the expansion and contraction of the gills, receiving the water and letting it pass through, fulfills the function of breathing. Fish have their own lot, their own nature, a separate way of life, a distinct manner of living. For this reason, none of the swimming creatures allows itself to be tamed, nor does it endure at all the touch of a human hand.

"Let the waters bring forth creeping things that are living creatures according to kind" (Genesis 1:20). He commands that the first beginnings of each kind be brought forth now, as seeds of nature, so to speak; their abundance is stored up for the succession that follows, when they must increase and multiply. One kind is what are called shell-skinned creatures: mussels, scallops, sea snails, conches, and the countless varieties of oysters. Another kind besides these is what are called soft-shelled creatures: crayfish, crabs, and those similar to them. Another kind besides these is the soft-bodied creatures, so named because their flesh is soft and yielding: octopuses, cuttlefish, and those like them. And among these again there are countless differences. For sea serpents, moray eels, and eels—which are found in muddy rivers and lakes—approach the poisonous reptiles more closely than fish in the similarity of their nature. One kind is that of egg-laying creatures, and another that of creatures bearing live young. The dogfish-like creatures and the small sharks bear live young, and in general the so-called cartilaginous fish. And most of the sea-monsters bear live young: dolphins and seals, which are said to receive their young back into the belly and shelter them when they are still young and frightened by some cause.

"Let the waters bring forth according to kind." The sea-monster kind is one thing, and the kind of small fish is another. Again, among fish there are countless differences divided according to kinds, with their own names, different food, shape, size, and qualities of flesh—all separated from one another by the greatest differences and established in different forms. What tuna-watchers, then, can enumerate for us the differences of the kinds? Yet they say that they can report the number of fish in great schools. And who among those who have grown old along the shores and coasts can make known to us the account of all of them with precision? Those who fish the Indian Ocean know some creatures; those who hunt the Egyptian gulf know others; islanders know others; and the Maurusians know others. But all alike, small and great, that first command and that ineffable power brought forth. Many are the variations of ways of life; many also are the differences in the succession of each kind. Most fish do not brood over their eggs as birds do, nor do they build nests, nor do they raise their young with labor; but the water receives the egg that falls out and makes it a living creature.
orientation: Basil is expounding the command 'Let the waters bring forth' from Genesis 1:20, explaining why fish are naturally suited to water and enumerating the kinds of water creatures.

title: Fish kinds, greed, and the crab's cunning
english: For each kind the succession is unchangeable and unmixed with another nature. It is not like the mules on dry land, or the couplings of certain birds that falsify the kinds. Among fish nothing is armed with teeth only halfway, as the ox is among us and the sheep; for nothing among them chews the cud, except the scarus alone, as some report. All of them are packed thick with the sharpest points of teeth, so that their food may not slip away through prolonged chewing; for if it were not cut up quickly and sent on to the stomach, it would be dissolved in the fine dividing by the water.

The food of fish is different for different kinds, marked out according to kind. Some feed on mud; others on seaweed; others are satisfied with the plants that grow in the water. But most fish are eaters of one another, and among them the smaller is food for the larger. And if it ever happens that the one that overpowered the smaller becomes the prey of another, they are brought under the single stomach of the last one. What then do we human beings do differently in our domination of those who are weaker? How does the man differ from the last fish, who with gluttonous love of wealth hides the weak in the insatiable folds of his greed? That one had what belonged to the poor man; you took this and made it part of your own surplus. You have shown yourself more unjust than the unjust, and more greedy than the greedy. Beware lest the same end as the fish await you—some hook, or weel, or net. For certainly we too, after passing through many acts of injustice, will not escape the final punishment.

Now that I have observed in a weak animal the great cunning and treachery, I want you to flee the imitation of evildoers. The crab desires the flesh of the oyster; but the catch is hard for it to make because of the shell's covering. For nature has secured the soft flesh with an unbreakable fence. This is why it is called shell-skinned. And since two hollows fitted precisely to each other enfold the oyster, the claws of the crab are necessarily ineffective. What then does it do? When it sees the oyster in windless places warming itself with pleasure, and spreading out its folds toward the ray of the sun, then it secretly slips in a pebble and prevents the closing, and the deficiency of its power is found to be supplied by its cunning. This is the wickedness of creatures that share neither reason nor voice. But I want you, admiring the resourceful ingenuity of crabs, to refrain from harming your neighbors. Such is the one who proceeds against his brother with deceit, and attacks his neighbors in their moments of vulnerability, and revels in the misfortunes of others. Flee the imitations of those who stand condemned. Be content with what is your own. Poverty with true self-sufficiency is more precious to the wise than every enjoyment.

I would not pass over the deceit and trickery of the octopus, which takes on the color of whatever rock it clings to at any given time. So most fish, swimming without foresight, fall upon the octopus as if it were the rock, and become ready prey for the cunning creature. Such in character are those who go along with the powers that always prevail, and adapt themselves to each occasion's needs, never standing on the same fixed purpose, but easily becoming different people at different times—honoring self-control among the self-controlled, but licentious among the licentious, shifting their judgments to please each person.
orientation: Basil continues his moral reading of sea creatures, contrasting the fixed kinds of fish with human greed and the craftiness of the crab and octopus.

title: Fish keep their bounds; humans do not
english: It is not easy to avoid such people, nor to guard against the harm they do, because their wickedness is deeply hidden under the guise of friendship. The Lord calls such characters ravenous wolves, appearing in garments of sheep (Matthew 7:15). Flee the varied and many-sided character; pursue truth, sincerity, simplicity. The serpent is subtle; for this reason it was condemned to crawl. The righteous man is without guile, like Jacob. For this reason the Lord settles the solitary in a home (Psalm 67:7 LXX (Hebrew 68:6)). This is the great and wide sea; there are creeping things without number, small animals with great (Psalm 103:25 LXX). Yet among them there is a wise and orderly arrangement. We cannot only find fault with fish; there are also things in them worth imitating. How is it that each kind of fish, having distributed to itself the region suited to it, does not encroach upon the others, but remains within its own boundaries? No surveyor among them divided up their dwellings; they are not marked off by walls; they are not separated by boundary stones; yet what is useful for each has been assigned to each automatically. This bay feeds certain kinds of fish, and that one others; and the kinds that multiply here are not found among others. No mountain rising with sharp peaks separates them, no river cuts off their passage, but there is a law of nature that allots to each its way of life equitably and justly according to what each needs.

But we are not like this. How could we be? We remove the ancient boundaries that our fathers set (Proverbs 22:28). We cut off land, we join house to house and field to field, so that we may take something from our neighbor (Isaiah 5:8). The sea monsters know the way of life marked out for them by nature; they have taken possession of the sea outside the inhabited regions, the desolate region of islands, where no continent stands opposite on the other side. For this reason it is unnavigable, since neither inquiry nor any need persuades sailors to venture upon it. The sea monsters, which in size resemble the greatest mountains, as those who have seen them say, have taken possession of that sea and remain within their own boundaries, harming neither the islands nor the coastal cities. So each kind, as if in cities or villages or ancient homelands, makes its dwelling in the parts of the sea assigned to it.

And some fish are migratory, as if setting out from a common council chamber for foreign territory; they all depart at a single signal. For when the appointed time of breeding arrives, different fish from different bays migrate, stirred by the common law of nature, and press on toward the northern sea. And at the time of their ascent you could see the fish united like a current, flowing through the Sea of Marmara toward the Black Sea. Who moves them? What king's command? What edicts posted in the marketplace announce the appointed time? Who are the guides? You see the divine order filling all things and extending through the smallest creatures. A fish does not oppose the law of God, and we human beings do not endure saving teachings. Do not despise fish because they are voiceless and completely without reason; rather, fear that you may be more without reason than they are, by resisting the command of the Creator. Listen to the fish, who all but utter a voice through what they do: we undertake this long journey for the continuance of our kind.
orientation: Basil is preaching on the fifth day's water creatures, drawing a moral contrast between the orderly behavior of fish and human greed.

title: Fish and sea urchin teach providence and marital fidelity
english: They have no reason of their own, but they have the law of nature strongly implanted in them, pointing out what must be done. "Let us go," they say, "to the northern sea." For its water is sweeter than the rest of the sea, because the sun spends only a little time upon it and does not draw out all its drinkable quality through its rays. Sea creatures also delight in sweet water; that is why they often swim up into rivers and travel far from the sea. For this reason the Black Sea is more prized by them than the other gulfs, as a place suited for hatching and rearing their young. But when the object of their eagerness has been sufficiently accomplished, all together in a body they all return home again. And what is the reason? Let us hear it from those who are silent. "The northern sea," they say, "is shallow, and lying flat and exposed to the forces of the winds, it has few shores and places of refuge. Therefore the winds easily turn it over from its very depths, so that even the sand from the bottom is mixed with the waves. It is also cold in the winter season, filled by many great rivers." For this reason, after enjoying it moderately in the summer, in winter they hasten again to the warmth in the deep and the sun-facing regions, and fleeing the storminess of the northern waters, they anchor in the gulfs that are less shaken.

I have seen these things myself, and I marveled at the wisdom of God in all things. If irrational creatures are inventive and protective of their own safety, and the fish knows what is to be chosen and what is to be avoided, what shall we say—we who have been honored with reason, instructed by law, urged on by promises, made wise by the Spirit—if we then manage our own affairs more irrationally than the fish? For they know how to exercise some forethought for the future, while we, through hopelessness about what is to come, consume our lives in a beast-like way. A fish crosses such vast seas to find some benefit. What will you say, you who live with idleness? Idleness is the beginning of wickedness. Let no one plead ignorance. A natural reason has been sown within us, showing us our kinship with the good and our alienation from harmful things.

I do not depart from the examples of the sea, since these are set before us for examination. I have heard from one of the coastal people that the sea urchin, that tiny and utterly contemptible creature, often becomes a teacher of calm and of storm to sailors. Whenever it foresees a disturbance from the winds, it gets under a sizable pebble and rides securely upon it as upon an anchor, held by the weight so that it is not easily dragged away by the waves. When sailors see this sign, they know that a violent movement of the winds is to be expected. No astrologer, no Chaldean, who infers disturbances of the air from the risings of the stars, taught these things to the urchin; rather, the Lord of the sea and the winds placed in this small creature a clear trace of his great wisdom. Nothing is without providence, nothing is neglected by God. The unsleeping eye watches over all things. He is present to all, providing safety for each one. If God did not leave the urchin outside his own care, does he not watch over your affairs?

Husbands, love your wives, even if you have come together from distant lands for the communion of marriage. Let the bond of nature, the yoke given through blessing, be the union of those who were separated.
orientation: Basil is preaching on the fifth day's water creatures, drawing moral lessons from fish migrations and the sea urchin's storm-sensing behavior.

title: The viper and the moray as marriage lessons
english: The viper, the most dangerous of reptiles, goes to meet the moray eel of the sea for marriage, and by hissing announces his presence, calling her up from the depths for the nuptial embrace. She obeys and unites herself with the venomous one. What does this account mean for me? That even if the housemate is harsh or savage in character, one must bear the yokemate and accept no pretext for tearing apart the union. Is he a striker? But he is a husband. Is he a drunkard? But he is united to you by nature. Is he harsh and hard to please? But he is already your member, and the most honored of your members.

Let the husband also hear the counsel that belongs to him. The viper vomits out its venom out of reverence for marriage; do you not put away the harshness and inhumanity of your soul out of reverence for the union? Perhaps the example of the viper will serve us in yet another way: the coupling of the viper and the moray eel is a kind of adultery against nature. Let those who plot against the marriages of others learn, then, what kind of reptile they resemble. My one aim is that the Church be built up from every side. Let the passions of the licentious be restrained, instructed by examples from land and sea.

Here the weakness of my body and the lateness of the hour compel me to stop my discourse, though I could still add many things worthy of wonder for those who love to hear—about the things that grow in the sea, and about the sea itself. How water solidifies into salt; how the precious stone, coral, is a plant in the sea, but when brought out into the air it hardens into the solidity of stone; from where nature placed the costly pearl inside the cheapest of creatures, the oyster. For the treasures that kings desire are scattered along shores and beaches and rough rocks, lying inside the shells of oysters. From where do the pinnae produce their golden wool, which no dyer of flowers has ever imitated until now? From where do the murex shells bestow their royal purple on kings, shells that have surpassed the flowers of the meadows in beauty of color?

"Let the waters bring forth" (Genesis 1:20). And what necessary thing has not come to be? What costly thing has not been granted to life? Some things are for the service of human beings; others are for the contemplation of the wonder in creation. Others are fearsome, disciplining our slackness.

"God made the great sea creatures" (Genesis 1:21). They are not called great merely because they are larger than a shrimp or a sprat, but because they rival the greatest mountains in the bulk of their bodies. They often present the appearance of islands whenever they swim up to the very surface of the water. Yet these creatures, enormous as they are, do not linger near shores or beaches, but inhabit the ocean called the Atlantic. Such are the animals created for our fear and astonishment.

But if you hear that the remora, the smallest little fish, so easily stops the largest ships sailing with spread sails and driven by a fair wind, keeping the vessel motionless for a very long time as if it were rooted in the middle of the sea—do you not receive in this small creature the same proof of the Creator's power? For not only swordfish, sawfish, dogfish, whales, and hammerhead sharks are fearsome, but also the stingray's barb, even when the stingray is dead, and the sea hare are no less fearsome, bringing swift and inescapable destruction.
orientation: Basil is drawing moral lessons from sea creatures, now using the viper and moray eel to teach spouses to endure each other and to warn adulterers.

title: The Creator's wonders on land and the transition to land animals
english: So through all these things the Creator wants you to stay awake, so that by your hope in God you may escape the harm they can do. But let us now run back up from the depths and flee for refuge to the mainland. For the wonders of creation, coming upon us one after another like waves, have led our discourse under water by their continuous and successive assaults. And yet I would be surprised if our mind, once it encounters the greater marvels of the land, does not again run away to the sea like Jonah. It seems to me that our discourse, having fallen among countless wonders, has forgotten its measure, and has suffered the same thing as those who sail on the open sea: with no fixed point by which to judge their movement, they often do not know how far they have traveled. This seems to have happened to us as well: as our discourse ran through creation, we did not perceive the sheer number of things said. But even if this august theater loves to listen, and the telling of the Master's wonders is sweet to the ears of His servants, let us anchor our discourse here and wait for the day to render what remains. And when we all rise, let us give thanks for what has been said, and ask for the completion of what remains. May there also be for you, in the partaking of your food, table-talk about all that came to you this morning and all that our discourse brought this evening. And may you be overtaken by sleep with thoughts about these things, so that even while sleeping you enjoy the daytime's gladness, and may it be possible for you to say, "I sleep, but my heart is awake," meditating night and day on the law of the Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen. Homily 8: On birds and water creatures. 8.1 And God said, "Let the earth bring forth a living creature according to kind: four-footed animals and creeping things and wild beasts according to kind." And it was so (Genesis 1:24). The command came walking along its path, and the earth received its own adornment. There, "Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living creatures" (Genesis 1:20); here, "Let the earth bring forth a living creature." Is the earth then ensouled? Do the foolish Manichaeans have any ground for putting a soul into the earth? It is not because He said "Let it bring forth" that the earth brought out what was stored up within it; rather, the One who gave the command also granted it the power to bring forth. For when the earth heard, "Let it sprout the herb of grass and the fruit tree" (Genesis 1:11), it did not bring out grass it had hidden within itself; it did not send up to the surface a palm tree or an oak or a cypress that had been stored away somewhere in its hollows. No, the divine word is the nature of the things that come to be. "Let the earth sprout": not "let it cast out what it has," but "let it acquire what it does not have," since God grants the power to be active. So now also, "Let the earth bring forth a living creature": not the one stored up within it, but the one given to it by God through the command. And then the argument will turn back against them in the opposite direction. For if the earth brought out the soul, it left itself bereft of soul. But their abomination is obvious immediately. Why, however, were the waters commanded to bring forth creeping things of living creatures, while the earth was commanded to bring forth a living creature? We reason, then, that the nature of swimming things seems to share in a life that is somehow less complete, because they live in the thickness of the water.
orientation: Basil is closing his homily on sea creatures and beginning the next homily, where he turns to the land animals created on the sixth day.

title: Souls of water creatures and land animals compared
english: For among water creatures hearing is dull, and their sight is blurred as they look through the water. They have no memory, no imagination, no recognition of what is familiar. This is why the text seems to indicate that for water creatures, fleshly life directs the movements of the soul, whereas for land animals, since their life is more complete, the soul has been entrusted with the entire leadership. For their senses are rather sharpened, and sharp are the perceptions of things present; and accurate are the memories of things past among most of the four-footed animals. So it seems that in the case of water creatures, ensouled bodies were created—for creeping things of living creatures were brought forth from the waters—but in the case of land animals, a soul managing bodies was commanded to come into being, since those that live on the earth have received a greater share of vital power. Land animals too are without reason, yet each one, by the voice nature gives it, signals many of the passions of the soul. By sound it reveals joy and grief, recognition of what is familiar, lack of food, separation from its companions, and countless other passions. But water creatures are not only voiceless; they are also wild, unteachable, and unmanageable for any shared life with human beings. The ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's manger (Isaiah 1:3), but a fish would not recognize the one who feeds it. The donkey knows the familiar voice. It knows the road it has often traveled, and sometimes it even becomes a guide for a person who has lost the way. And no other land animal is said to have hearing as sharp as this creature. As for the camel's holding of grudges, its heavy anger, its lasting rage—what sea creature could imitate that? A camel struck once long ago stores up its wrath for a long time, and when it finds the opportunity, it pays back the harm. Listen, you who are slow to forgive, you who cultivate the holding of grudges as if it were a virtue: whom do you resemble when you guard your grief against your neighbor like a spark hidden in ashes, until you find fuel and kindle your anger into a flame?

"Let the earth bring forth a living creature" (Genesis 1:24). Why does the earth bring forth a living creature? So that you may learn the difference between the soul of an animal and the soul of a human being. A little later you will learn how the human soul was constituted; for now, hear about the soul of creatures without reason. Since, as it is written, the soul of every living creature is its blood (Leviticus 17:11), and blood when it congeals naturally changes into flesh, and flesh when it decays dissolves into earth, the soul of animals is reasonably something earthy. "Let the earth bring forth a living creature," then. Observe the sequence: soul to blood, blood to flesh, flesh to earth. And again, reversing the steps, go back from earth to flesh, from flesh to blood, from blood to soul, and you will find that the soul of animals is earth. Do not think that it is older than the substance of their body, or that it remains after the dissolution of the flesh. Flee the nonsense of the pompous philosophers, who are not ashamed to make their own souls and the souls of bitches of the same kind as one another—who say that they themselves were once women, and bushes, and fish of the sea.
orientation: Basil is comparing the souls of water creatures with those of land animals, arguing that land animals have a fuller share of psychic life, and he is about to explain why the earth is commanded to bring forth a living creature.

title: The omitted birds must be treated
english: Now I would not say that I myself was ever a fish, but I would maintain most vigorously that in the passage where I was writing these things, I was more irrational than the fish. “Let the earth bring forth a living creature” (Genesis 1:24). Why, when the discourse was running on so swiftly, did I fall silent for no small time? Perhaps many are wondering, but the more diligent among my hearers know the cause of my speechlessness. How? They are the ones who, by looking at one another and nodding, turned me back to themselves and brought to mind what had been passed over. For a whole class of creation, and not the least important one, had escaped us, and the discourse nearly went on its way leaving it completely unexamined. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying over the earth across the firmament of heaven according to kind” (Genesis 1:20). We spoke about the swimming creatures, as much as the evening allowed; today we moved on to the examination of the land animals. The winged creature slipped through in the middle. So then, like forgetful travelers who, when they leave behind something essential, even if they have gone far along the road, turn back again, paying the penalty for their carelessness with the toil of the journey—so we too, it seems, must walk the same road again. For what was passed over is not something to be despised; it seems to be a third part of the creation of living things, if indeed there are three kinds of living creatures: the land animal, the winged, and the water-dwelling. “Let the waters bring forth,” it says, “creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying over the earth across the firmament of heaven according to kind” (Genesis 1:20). Why did he give the winged creatures their origin from the waters? Because there is a certain kinship between flying creatures and swimming creatures. For just as fish cut through the water, moving forward by the motion of their wings, and steering their turns and straight courses by the movement of their tail, so also in the case of winged creatures one can see them swimming through the air with their wings in a similar way. Therefore, since swimming is one distinctive property in both, a single kinship was provided for them from their origin in the waters. Except that no winged creature is footless, because all of them have their sustenance from the earth, and all necessarily require the service of feet. For the predatory ones have sharp points of claws for the hunt; for the rest, the service of feet has been granted as necessary both for procuring food and for the rest of life's conduct. But a few birds are bad-footed, suited neither for walking nor for hunting with their feet—as the swallows are, unable either to walk or to hunt, and the so-called scythe-birds, whose food is contrived from things carried in the air. For the swallow, its low flight near the ground takes the place of the service of feet. There are, however, countless differences of kinds among the birds, which if someone examines in the same way that we partially took up the examination of the fish, he will find that there is one name for winged creatures, but countless differences among them in sizes and in shapes and in colors; and in their ways of life, their activities, and their habits, their variation from one another is beyond telling.
orientation: Basil is preaching on the creation of animals and has just discussed land animals, but he realizes he skipped the birds, which were created on the fifth day from the waters.

title: Kinds of birds and the polity of bees
english: Some people have already tried to use name-makings, so that the distinctive character of each kind might be recognized through these unfamiliar and strange names, as if by branding marks. They called some split-winged, like the eagles; others skin-winged, like the bats; others feathered, like the wasps; others sheath-winged, like the beetles and all those that are born inside certain cases and coverings, and when their sheath breaks open they are set free for flight. But for us, common usage is a sufficient indication of the distinctiveness of the kinds, along with the distinctions in Scripture concerning clean and unclean creatures.

So one kind is that of the flesh-eaters, and their equipment is suited to their manner of life: sharp talons, a hooked beak, and a pointed wing, so that the prey can be seized easily and, once torn apart, become food for the one who caught it. The equipment of the seed-pickers is different; that of those that feed on whatever they happen to find is different again. And among these there are very many differences.

Some of them are gregarious, except for the predatory ones; none of these is social except for the pairing of mates. Countless others have chosen the life of the flock, like doves, cranes, starlings, and jackdaws. Again, among these some have no ruler and are, so to speak, self-governing; others accept being arranged under a leader, like the cranes. And there is yet another difference among them, according to which some are stay-at-home and native to a place, while others are by nature inclined to depart very far, and for the most part to move away when winter approaches.

Many birds, when raised by hand, become tame and domesticated—except, of course, the weak ones, which because of their excessive timidity and lack of spirit cannot endure the constant disturbance of the hand. But some birds are human-companionable, accepting the same dwellings as we do; others are mountain-dwellers and lovers of solitude. The greatest difference is also the distinctive character of each one's voice. Some birds are chatterers and talkative; others are silent. Some are songful and have many voices; others are entirely without music and have no share in song. Some are imitative, either having the ability to imitate by nature or acquiring it through practice; others send forth a voice of one single type, unchangeable.

The rooster is proud; the peacock is a lover of beauty; doves and domestic hens are lustful, having the impulse to mate at every season. The partridge is deceitful and jealous, working knavishly with the hunters toward the capture.

There are countless differences, as we said, in their activities and their ways of life. And there are even some political ones among the irrational creatures—if indeed the mark of a political community is that the activity of each individual converges toward one common end, as one might see in the case of the bees. For their dwelling is common, their flight is common, and the work of all is one; and what is greatest, they set about their tasks under a king and a commander of some sort, not consenting to go out to the meadows until they see the king take the lead in flight. And their king is not elected by vote—for often the poor judgment of the people has set the worst man in power—nor does he hold his authority by lot, for the chances of the lot are irrational and often bring power to the lowest of all; nor does he sit in the royal palace by paternal succession, for such kings also become uneducated and ignorant of every virtue, for the most part through luxury and flattery. Rather, he has his preeminence over all from nature, excelling in size and in form and in the gentleness of his character.
orientation: Basil is still expounding the fifth day's creation of birds, now surveying differences among bird kinds and then turning to bees as an example of political order among irrational creatures.

title: The bee's sting, honeycomb geometry, and the order of cranes and storks
english: The king does have a sting, but he does not use it for self-defense. These are unwritten laws of nature: that those who mount the greatest powers are slow to punish. And among the bees, any that do not follow the example of the king quickly regret their folly, because they die upon the blow of the sting. Let Christians hear this—Christians who have the command to repay no one evil for evil, but to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17, 21). Imitate the peculiar character of the bee: it harms no one, it destroys no one else's fruit, and yet it builds its combs. For it gathers the wax openly from the flowers, and the honey—the dew-like moisture scattered in the flowers—it draws in with its mouth and pours into the hollows of the combs. At first the honey is liquid; then, ripened by time, it returns to its own proper consistency and sweetness. This bee has received fine and fitting praise from Proverbs, where it is called wise and a worker (Proverbs 6:8)—so industriously does it gather its food (whose labors, it says, kings and common people alike consume for their health), and so wisely does it craft its storehouses of honey. For it stretches the wax into a thin membrane and builds the hollows close together and continuous with one another, so that the density of the tiny cells bound to each other becomes a support for the whole. Each little cell holds to the next, separated from it by a thin dividing wall and at the same time joined to it. Then these tubes are built upon one another in two and three stories. The bee has been careful not to make one hollow running straight through, so that the liquid does not escape to the outside under its own weight. Learn how the discoveries of geometry are the by-work of the most wise bee. All the tubes of the combs are hexagonal and equal-sided, and they do not lie directly on top of one another, so that the bottoms do not suffer strain when fitted onto empty gaps. Rather, the angles of the hexagons below serve as a base and support for those above, so that they safely hold up the weights above them, and the liquid is contained separately in each hollow.

How could I go through for you in detail all the distinctive traits in the lives of birds? How the cranes take up the night watches in turn: some sleep, while others circle around and provide them with complete safety in their sleep; then, when the time of the watch is fulfilled, the one that has called out turns to sleep, and the one that takes over the succession gives back in turn the safety it received. You will see this same good order in their flight. For at different times a different crane takes up the lead, and after guiding the flight for a fixed time, it moves to the rear and hands over the leadership of the way to the one behind it. The behavior of the storks is not far from rational understanding: they all arrive in these regions at one and the same season, and they all depart at one and the same signal. Our crows escort them and accompany them, providing, it seems to me, a kind of alliance against hostile birds. The proof is, first, that no crow appears at all during that season, and second, that when they return with wounds, they carry clear signs of the battle fought and the defense given.
orientation: Basil is continuing his survey of the natural world, now describing the bee's restraint and craftsmanship, then turning to the orderly behavior of cranes and storks as moral examples for Christians.

title: Birds as moral teachers: hospitality, care for parents, poverty, and providence
english: Who defined the laws of hospitality among them? Who threatened them with a charge of desertion, so that not one of them fails to join the escort? Let the inhospitable listen—those who shut their doors and do not even share a roof with travelers in winter and at night. The care storks show for their aged parents would be enough to make our children lovers of their fathers, if they were willing to pay attention. For surely no one is so lacking in understanding as to think it not worthy of shame to fall behind the most irrational birds in virtue. When the father has shed his feathers from old age, they stand around him in a circle and warm him with their own feathers, and they provide food in abundance, and they give him all the help they can in flight, gently lifting him on either side with their wings. And this is so widely celebrated that some people already call the repayment of benefits 'antipelargosis.' Let no one lament poverty; let no one despair of his life who has left no wealth at home, when he looks at the swallow's ingenuity. For when she builds her nest, she carries the twigs in her mouth; and since she cannot lift mud with her feet, she wets the tips of her wings with water, then rolls them in the finest dust, and in this way she devises the use of mud. And little by little she binds the twigs together with the mud as with a kind of glue, and in it she raises her young. If someone pierces out their eyes, she has a certain healing remedy from nature, through which she restores the sight of her offspring to health. Let these things admonish you not to turn to wickedness because of poverty, and not to cast away all hope in the most grievous sufferings and lie idle and inactive, but to flee to God—who, if he grants such great things to the swallow, how much greater things will he give to those who call upon him from a whole heart? The halcyon is a sea bird. It naturally nests on the very shores, laying its eggs on the sand itself; and it nests around the middle of winter, when the sea is dashed against the land by many violent winds. But nevertheless all the winds are lulled to sleep, and the sea wave is still, whenever the halcyon broods for the seven days. For in only so many days it hatches out its young. And since they also need food, the God who gives great gifts granted another seven days to the smallest creature for the growth of the young. So all sailors know this, and they call those days the halcyon days. These things have been ordained for you as an encouragement to ask God for the things that lead to salvation, through God's providence for the irrational creatures. What paradoxical thing would not happen for your sake, you who have been made according to the image of God, when for the sake of so small a bird the great and fearful sea is held back, commanded to keep calm in the middle of winter? 8.6 They say that the turtledove, once separated from her mate, no longer accepts union with another, but remains unpaired, refusing union with another out of memory of the one to whom she was once joined. Let women hear how the dignity of widowhood is preferred, even among irrational creatures, to the indecency of polygamy. The eagle is most unjust in the rearing of its young. For when it has brought out two chicks, it dashes one of them down to the ground, thrusting it away with blows of its wings; and taking up only the other one, it makes it its own, rejecting the one it begat because of the painful toil of feeding.
orientation: Basil continues his survey of bird behavior, drawing moral lessons for his congregation from the stork, swallow, halcyon, turtledove, and eagle.

title: Birds as moral examples and the fifth day command
english: But the vulture, they say, does not allow it to perish. It takes the chick up and rears it together with its own young. Such are those parents who expose their infants on the pretext of poverty, or who are most unfair to their offspring in the division of an inheritance. For it is right that, just as they have given each one a share in being equally, so they should provide the means for living to them equally and with equal honor. Do not imitate the cruelty of the birds with curved talons. When they see their young now daring to fly, they drive them out of the nest, striking them with their wings and pushing them, and they take no further care of them. The love of the crow for its young is praiseworthy: it accompanies them even when they are already flying, feeding them and rearing them for a very long time. Many kinds of birds need no intercourse with males for conception. In other birds the wind-eggs are infertile, but they say that vultures for the most part give birth without pairing, and these are very long-lived; their life extends for the most part to a hundred years. Keep this noted down for yourself from the study of birds, so that whenever you see people laughing at our mystery, as though it were impossible and outside nature for a virgin to give birth while her virginity remains undefiled, you may remember that the One who was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of the proclamation (1 Corinthians 1:21) prepared in advance countless starting points from nature for faith in things beyond expectation. "Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls, and winged creatures flying upon the earth, across the firmament of heaven" (Genesis 1:20). They were commanded to fly upon the earth because food for all comes from the earth. And "across the firmament of heaven," as we have already explained, because the air is here called "heaven" from being seen, and "firmament" because the air above our heads is somehow denser in comparison with the ethereal body, and more compressed by the exhalations from below. You have, then, a heaven adorned, an earth beautified, a sea teeming with its own offspring, an air full of the birds that fly through it. All things were brought by the command of God from non-being into being. And whatever the discourse has now passed over, avoiding a longer dwelling on these matters so as not to seem to exceed its measure, you who love labor should reason out for yourself, learning the wisdom of God in all things, and never cease from wonder, nor from glorifying the Maker through all creation. You have in the darkness the night-roaming kinds of birds; in the light, those that go about by day. Bats, owls, and night-ravens are among the night-dwellers. So when sleep is not present at some time, it is enough for you to spend time on these things and to examine the properties they possess for the glorification of the Maker. How sleepless the nightingale is when she sits on her eggs, not ceasing from her song through the whole night. How the bat is at once four-footed and winged. How it alone among birds uses teeth, and gives birth to live young like four-footed animals, and floats upon the air, not lifted by a wing, but by a certain membrane of skin.
orientation: Basil is still expounding the moral lessons from birds, then moves to the fifth day of creation when God commands the waters to bring forth living creatures and birds.

title: Wonders of birds and insects
english: Consider too how this mutual-loving trait exists in their nature: bats cling to one another like a string, each hanging from the next—a thing not easy for us human beings to achieve. For what is detached and private is preferred to what is shared and united with the many. How like the eyes of the owl are those who devote themselves to vain wisdom. The owl's sight is strong at night, but when the sun shines it grows dim. So too their mind is sharpest for contemplating vanity, but for perceiving the true light it has been dimmed.

By day it is very easy for you to gather wonder at the Creator from every side. The bird that lives with you rouses you to work, crying out with a sharp voice and announcing from afar that the sun is approaching, rousing travelers at dawn alongside them and leading farmers out to the harvest. How sleepless is the race of geese, and how sharp their perception of things that escape notice—they once even saved the royal city, revealing enemies who were already about to seize the citadel of Rome through hidden tunnels underground.

In what kind of birds does nature not display some wonder of its own? Who announces to vultures the death of human beings, when they march to war against one another? You could see countless flocks of vultures following the armies, inferring the outcome from the preparation of weapons. This is not far from human reasoning.

How shall I describe to you the fearful campaigns of the locust, which rises all at once at a single signal and encamps across the breadth of the land, and does not touch the crops until the divine command has been given to it? How does the seleucis bird follow as a remedy for the plague, possessing an endless power of eating, since the God who loves humankind made its nature insatiable for the benefit of human beings?

What is the manner of the cicada's song? And how are they more musical at midday, by the drawing of air that they make in the expansion of the chest, as the sound is given forth? But I seem to fall further behind in my account of the wonder of winged creatures than if I tried to reach their speed with my feet.

When you see the winged creatures called insects, such as bees and wasps—for they have been named this because they show incisions on every side—consider that these have no breath and no lung, but are nourished entirely through their whole body by the air. Therefore they are destroyed when dipped in oil, since their pores are blocked; but when vinegar is applied at once, they revive again, since the passages are opened. Our God created nothing superfluous to need, nor lacking in any necessity.

Again, when you study the water-loving animals, you will find a different construction in them: feet that are neither split, like those of the crow, nor hooked, like those of flesh-eaters, but broad and membrane-like, so that they may swim easily on the water, pushing through the liquid with the membranes of their feet as with oars. And if you observe how the swan lowers its neck into the deep and brings up its food from below, then you will discover the wisdom of the Creator—that for this reason he gave it a neck longer than its feet, so that, letting it down like a fishing line, it may procure the food hidden in the depth.
orientation: Basil is still expounding the fifth day's creation of birds and water creatures, drawing moral and theological lessons from their natural behaviors.

title: The wonder of winged creatures and the profit of staying
english: Read simply, the words of Scripture are only small syllables: “Let the waters bring forth winged creatures flying upon the earth along the firmament of heaven” (Genesis 1:20). But when the meaning within the words is searched out, then the great wonder of the Creator’s wisdom is revealed. How many varieties of birds did he foresee? How did he separate them from one another according to kind? How did he mark each one with distinct characteristics? The day fails me as I describe to you the wonders of the air. The dry land calls us to the display of wild beasts, reptiles, and cattle, ready to show in return creatures equal in honor to the plants, the swimming kind, and all the birds. “Let the earth bring forth the living creature of cattle and wild beasts and reptiles according to kind” (Genesis 1:24). What do you say, you who disbelieve Paul about the change at the resurrection, when you see many of the creatures of the air changing their forms? Such is the story told about the horned Indian worm: it first changes into a caterpillar, then as it advances becomes a chrysalis, and it does not stop at this form, but is furnished with wings of loose and broad leaf-like scales.
