So when you women sit unwinding the work of these creatures—I mean the threads the Chinese send you for the making of soft garments—remember the change of this animal, and receive a vivid conception of the resurrection, and do not disbelieve the change that Paul proclaims to all. But I sense that my discourse is going beyond its proper measure. When I look at the abundance of what has been said, I see myself carried beyond the limit; but when I look again at the variety of wisdom in the created works, I think I have not even begun the account. And at the same time, keeping you here longer is not without benefit. For what would one do with the time until evening? No hosts are pressing you; no banquets await you. Therefore, if it seems good, let us use the bodily fast for the gladness of our souls. You have often served the flesh for enjoyment; today remain in the service of the soul. Take delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart (Psalm 36:4 LXX). If you love wealth, you have spiritual wealth: the judgments of the Lord, the true ones, justified altogether, desirable beyond gold and much precious stone (Psalm 18:10-11 LXX [Hebrew 19:9-10]). If you love enjoyment and pleasure, you have the words of God, which to the one strong in spiritual perception are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Psalm 18:11 LXX [Hebrew 19:10]). If I dismiss you and dissolve the assembly, some will run to the dice. There are oaths, harsh quarrels, and the pangs of greed. A demon stands by, kindling madness through the marked bones, shifting the same money to one side or the other—now lifting this one up with victory and filling that one with gloom, then showing that one exulting and this one put to shame. What profit is there in fasting in the body while the soul is filled with countless evils? The one who does not gamble but passes his leisure otherwise—what vain things does he not utter? What absurd things does he not hear? For leisure without the fear of God is a teacher of wickedness to those who use their time badly. Perhaps, then, some benefit will be found in what has been said; but if not, at least the avoidance of sin comes to you from your occupation here.
orientation: Basil is preaching on the fifth day's creation of birds and water creatures, and now turns to the wonder of winged creatures, then urges his hearers to stay for spiritual nourishment rather than idle pursuits.

title: Defense of literal reading of creation
english: So the longer I hold you here, the longer I withdraw you from evils. What I have said is enough for a fair-minded judge—unless he looks not at the wealth of creation but at the weakness of my own ability, and at what is sufficient for the joy of those who have gathered. The earth welcomed you with its own plants; the sea with its fish; the air with its birds. The dry land is ready to display in return things equal in honor to these. But let this be the measure of the morning feast, so that excessive fullness does not make you dull for the enjoyment of the evening. May he who filled all things with his creation, and who left in all things clear reminders of his own wonders for us, fill your hearts with all spiritual joy, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, forever and ever. Amen.
HOMILY 9: On Land Animals

How did the morning table of words appear to you? For my part, it occurred to me to compare my own efforts to the hospitality of some poor host who, eager to be thought a fine entertainer, wearies his guests by the lack of costlier dishes, piling his meager provisions lavishly on the table—so that his ambition turns into a reproach for tastelessness. Something like that is true of us too, unless you say otherwise. But whatever it may be, you must not despise it. For the people of that time did not reject Elisha as a poor host, even though he entertained his friends with wild vegetables.

I know the rules of allegory—not because I discovered them myself, but because I have encountered the labors of others. Those who do not accept the ordinary meanings of what is written say that water is not water but some other nature, and they interpret plant and fish according to their own fancy, and they explain the origin of reptiles and wild beasts by twisting them into their own private notions—just as dream interpreters make their explanations of what appears in sleep-visions fit their own purpose. But when I hear grass, I understand grass, and plant, and fish, and wild beast, and cattle—I take everything just as it is said. For I am not ashamed of the gospel (Romans 1:16).

Nor is it because those who have written about the world have said many things about the shapes of the earth—whether the earth is a sphere, or a cylinder, or like a disk, and whether it is turned equally on all sides, or is winnowing-fan-shaped and hollow in the middle (for the writers about the world have been carried into all these notions, each one demolishing the others)—I will not for that reason be led to call our world-making less honorable, just because Moses, the servant of God, said nothing about shapes, nor said that the earth's circumference is one hundred eighty thousand stadia, nor measured how far its shadow extends through the air when the sun moves beneath the earth, nor how this shadow, when it reaches the moon, produces eclipses. Since he passed over in silence the things that are of no use to us, shall I for this reason consider the oracles of the Spirit less honorable than the wisdom that has been made foolish (1 Corinthians 1:20)? Or rather, shall I glorify him who did not occupy our minds with vain things, but arranged for everything to be written for the building up and perfecting of our souls? Some people, it seems to me, have not understood this, and with certain derivations and figurative interpretations they have attempted to attach a certain dignity from their own thinking to what is written.
orientation: Basil is closing the eighth homily and opening the ninth, defending his literal reading of Genesis against allegorizers.

title: The earth's command to bring forth living creatures
english: But this is what someone does when he makes himself wiser than the oracles of the Spirit, and under the pretense of interpretation smuggles in his own ideas. Let it be understood, then, as it is written.

“Let the earth bring forth the living creature of cattle and wild beasts and creeping things” (Genesis 1:24). Consider the word of God running through creation, beginning then and still at work now, and pressing on to a prosperous end until the world is completed. For just as a ball, when someone pushes it and it finds a slope, is carried downhill by its own construction and the suitability of the ground, and does not stop until something level receives it, so the nature of existing things, set in motion by a single command, passes evenly through the creation that is subject to birth and decay, preserving the successions of kinds through likeness, until it arrives at the end itself. For it makes a horse the successor of a horse, and a lion of a lion, and an eagle of an eagle, and it hands on each of the animals, preserved through successive generations, until the completion of all things. No time corrupts or makes obsolete the distinctive traits of animals, but their nature, as if just now established, always fresh, runs along with time.

“Let the earth bring forth the living creature.” This command remained in the earth, and it does not cease serving the Creator. For some creatures are brought forth from the succession of those that existed before, but others are shown even now to be generated alive from the earth itself. For not only does it send up cicadas in rainy seasons, and countless other kinds of winged creatures borne in the air, most of which are nameless because of their smallness, but it already also produces mice and frogs from itself. Indeed, around Thebes in Egypt, whenever it rains heavily in the heat, the country is immediately filled with field mice. And we see that eels are formed in no other way than from the mud; neither an egg nor any other method establishes their succession, but their origin is from the earth.

“Let the earth bring forth the living creature.” The cattle are earthy and bent toward the ground, but man, the heavenly plant, differs as much in the dignity of his soul as in the shape of his bodily form. What is the shape of the four-footed animals? Their head is bent down toward the earth, it looks toward the belly, and it pursues the belly's pleasure in every way. Your head stands upright toward heaven; your eyes look upward. So if you ever dishonor yourself with the passions of the flesh, serving the belly and the parts beneath it, you have been grouped with the senseless cattle and have become like them. A different concern befits you: to seek the things above, where Christ is (Colossians 3:1-2), and to be above earthly things in your mind. As you have been shaped, so order your life as well. Have your citizenship in heaven (Philippians 3:20). Your true homeland is the Jerusalem above, and your fellow citizens and kin are the firstborn, enrolled in heaven (Hebrews 12:22-23).

“Let the earth bring forth the living creature.” The soul of the irrational animals, then, was not stored up in the earth and then revealed, but came into existence together with the command. And the soul of the irrational animals is one. For the one thing that characterizes it is irrationality.
orientation: Basil is expounding Genesis 1:24, where God commands the earth to bring forth living creatures, and is contrasting the earth-bound posture of animals with the heavenward posture of man.

title: Each animal's natural character and the lessons for humans
english: Each animal is distinguished by its own characteristics. The ox is steady, the donkey sluggish; the horse is hot in its desire for the female; the wolf is untamable, and the fox is cunning; the deer is timid; the ant is industrious; the dog is grateful and remembers friendship. For each was created at the same moment, and it brought along with itself the characteristic of its nature. The lion's anger was born together with it, along with its solitary way of life and its not sharing communion with its own kind. For like some tyrant among the irrational animals, because of its natural arrogance it does not accept equal honor with the many. It does not even accept yesterday's food, nor would it even go near the remains of its own hunt. Nature has placed in it such powerful organs of voice that many animals that surpass it in speed are often caught by the roar alone. The leopard is impetuous and swift in its impulses; its body has been joined to it as suitable, following the movements of its soul with suppleness and lightness. The bear's nature is sluggish, and its character is peculiar, deceitful, deeply hidden. Its body is clothed to match: heavy, compact, without joints, fitting for a creature that is actually a den-dweller, chilled. If we go through in our discussion how much untaught and natural care for their own life exists in these irrational animals, we shall either be moved toward guarding ourselves and providing for the salvation of our souls, or we shall be condemned all the more when we are found falling short even of imitating the irrational animals. A bear, often wounded with the deepest gashes, heals itself, stopping up its wounds by every means with the mullein plant, whose nature is dry. You could also see a fox healing itself with the resin of the pine tree. A tortoise, when it has gorged on viper flesh, escapes the harm of the venom through the antidote of oregano. And a snake heals the damage in its eyes by feeding on fennel. And what rational understanding do the animals' forecasts of changes in the weather not reveal? The sheep, when winter is approaching, takes in its food greedily, as if storing up provisions for the coming scarcity. Cattle that have been shut up for a long time in the winter season, when spring is already approaching, perceive the change by natural sensation and look from their stalls toward the exits, all shifting their posture at a single signal. And already some industrious people have observed that the land hedgehog makes two breathing holes in its burrow, and when the north wind is about to blow, it blocks up the one facing north; but when the south wind takes over again, it moves to the one facing south. What is being shown to us human beings through these things? Not only that the care of our Creator extends through all things, but also that among the irrational animals there is some perception of the future, so that we too should not cling to the present life, but should have all our zeal for the age to come. Will you not labor on your own behalf, O man? Will you not store up beforehand in the present age the rests of the age to come, looking to the example of the ant? It treasures up its winter food in summer, and not because the hardships of winter are not yet here does it let the time pass in idleness; but with an unrelenting eagerness it strains toward the work, until it has stored away sufficient food in its chambers. And it does not do this carelessly, but by some wise contrivance it makes the food last as long as possible.
orientation: Basil is describing how each kind of animal was created with its own distinctive natural character, and then draws moral lessons from their instinctive care for themselves.

title: Nature's untaught wisdom and the soul's natural virtues
english: For it cuts through the very middle of the grains with its own claws, so that they will not sprout and become useless to it for food. And it dries them out whenever it perceives that they are soaked through. It does not bring them out at every season, but only when it perceives beforehand that the air is holding in a fair-weather condition. Indeed, you would not see rain pouring from the clouds for as long as the grain has been brought out by the ants. What speech could reach all this? What hearing could contain it? What time would be enough to tell and recount all the wonders of the Craftsman? Let us too say with the prophet, “How great are your works, O Lord; in wisdom you made them all” (Psalm 104:24, LXX Psalm 103:24). So it is not enough for our defense that we were not taught what is beneficial by letters, since we have received the choice of what is advantageous by the untaught law of nature. Do you know what good you will do to your neighbor? What you wish to have done to yourself by another. Do you know what evil is? What you yourself would not choose to suffer from another. No root-cutting skill and no botanical experience discovered the teaching of what is beneficial for the irrational animals. Rather, each of the animals is naturally resourceful for providing its own safety, and possesses a certain inexpressible affinity for what is according to nature. 9.4 There are also among us virtues according to nature, toward which the soul’s affinity exists not from human teaching but from nature itself. For just as no argument teaches us to hate sickness, but we have an automatic aversion to what causes pain, so too the soul has a certain untaught avoidance of evil. Every evil is a sickness of the soul, and virtue holds the place of health. For some have well defined health as the stability of the natural activities. If one says this also about the good condition of the soul, he will not miss what is fitting. From this the soul is, without teaching, desiring of what is its own and according to nature. Therefore temperance is praised by all, and justice is accepted, and courage is admired, and prudence is eagerly sought. These are more akin to the soul than health is to the body. Children, love your fathers. Parents, do not provoke your children. Does not nature itself say these things? Paul urges nothing new, but tightens the bonds of nature. If the lioness loves her offspring, and the wolf fights for its pups, what can a person say who both disobeys the commandment and falsifies nature, when either a child dishonors the old age of a father, or a father through a second marriage forgets his earlier children? The mutual affection of children and parents toward one another is irresistible in the irrational animals, because the God who created them compensated for the lack of reason through the abundance of their senses. For how is it that among countless sheep a lamb, leaping out from the folds, knows the very color and the voice of its mother, and hurries toward her, and seeks out its own fountains of milk? And if it happens upon its mother’s poor teats, it is content with those, having run past many heavy udders. And how does the mother among countless lambs recognize her own? The voice is one, the color the same, the smell alike from all, as far as it presents itself to our sense of smell—but nevertheless there is in them a perception sharper than our comprehension, by which each one has the recognition of its own.
orientation: Basil is drawing moral lessons from animal behavior, arguing that animals know by nature what preserves them, and now extends this to the soul's natural inclination toward virtue.

title: Animal instincts and anatomy show the Creator's wisdom
english: The puppy does not yet have teeth, and yet it defends itself with its mouth against whatever hurts it. The calf does not yet have horns, and yet it knows where its weapons will grow in. These things prove that the natures of all creatures are untaught, and that nothing among existing things is disordered or undefined, but all things bear traces of the wisdom of their Maker, showing in themselves that they were brought forth equipped beforehand for the guarding of their own safety. The dog has no share in reason, but nevertheless it has a perception equal in power to reason. For what the wise men of the world, sitting down over the long leisure of their lives, have barely discovered—I mean the tangles of syllogisms—the dog is shown to have been taught by nature. For when it searches out the track of a wild animal and finds it split in many directions, it goes over the turnings that lead each way, and all but lets out the syllogistic voice through what it does: either the animal turned this way, it says, or that way, or toward this other part; but it did not turn this way or that way; therefore it remains that it rushed off that way. And so by the removal of the false things it finds the true thing. What more do those who sit solemnly over their diagrams and scratch in the dust accomplish, when they remove two of three propositions and discover the truth in the one that remains? And as for the memory of gratitude in this animal, which of the ungrateful toward their benefactors does it not put to shame? Many dogs are remembered for having died together with their masters when they were murdered in a deserted place. And some, while their grief was still fresh, even became guides to those searching for the murderers, and caused the criminals to be brought to trial. What will they say—those who not only do not love the Lord who made them and feeds them, but even treat as friends those who speak injustice against God, and share the same table with them, and put up with blasphemies against the One who feeds them right at the very meal? But let us return to the contemplation of creation. The animals that are more easily caught are more prolific. For this reason hares are prolific, and wild goats and wild sheep bear twins, so that the kind may not fail when it is consumed by flesh-eaters. But those that destroy others bear few young. Hence a lioness is barely the mother of one lion. For the lion tears the womb apart with the points of its claws and so comes forth, as they say; and vipers come forth by eating through the womb, paying back fitting wages to the mother that bore them. So nothing among existing things is without providence, nor without the care that belongs to it. And if you study the very limbs of animals, you will find that the Creator neither added anything superfluous nor removed anything necessary. To the flesh-eating animals he fitted sharp teeth; for such teeth were needed for the kind of food they eat. But those that are only half armed with teeth he prepared with many and varied storehouses of food. For because their food is not sufficiently ground up at the first pass, he gave them the ability to bring back up what they have swallowed, so that, after it is ground fine by chewing the cud, it may be assimilated to the one being nourished. Stomachs and omasums, and net-like stomachs, and rennet stomachs are not placed idly in the animals that have them, but each one fulfills the need of necessary functions. The neck of the camel is long, so that it may be equal to its feet and reach the grass on which it lives.
orientation: Basil is still expounding the fifth day's creatures, arguing that even brute animals display innate wisdom and that every part of their bodies is fitted by the Creator for their needs.

title: The elephant's fitted frame and the wisdom in small creatures
english: The bear's neck is short and sunk into its shoulders, and so is the lion's, and the tiger's, and the rest of that kind, because their food does not come from grass and they have no need to bend down to the ground, since they are flesh-eaters and sustain themselves by hunting other animals. What is the purpose of the elephant's trunk? Because the animal is large—the largest of the land animals—and was brought forth to terrify whatever it meets, its body had to be massive and compacted. If a neck as large and proportionate to its feet had been added to this body, the animal would have been hard to manage, always dragged downward by its excessive weight. As it is, the head is joined to the spine by only a few vertebrae of the neck, and it has the trunk, which fulfills the function of a neck: through it the elephant brings food to its mouth and draws up its drink. Its feet, moreover, are unjointed, like solid pillars, to support the weight. For if its limbs had been set beneath it loose and flexible, its joints would have been constantly dislocated, since they could not bear the weight when the animal crouched down and rose up again. As it is, a short ankle-bone lies under the elephant's foot, and it is not jointed either at the bend or at the knee. For the slipperiness of joints could never have endured the great mass of flesh poured around the animal and quivering on every side. Hence the need for that trunk that reaches down to its feet. Do you not see in wars how they go before the battle-line like living towers, or like hills of flesh, and with their irresistible onset they break through the shield-wall of the enemy? If their lower parts were not proportionate, the animal would not have survived for any length of time. As it is, some report that the elephant lives three hundred years and more; for this reason its limbs are solidly fixed and not jointed. Its food, as we said, the trunk carries up from the ground to the height—a trunk that is serpent-like and rather supple by nature. So true is the saying that nothing superfluous and nothing lacking can be found among created things. This animal, though so great in size, God has made subject to us—so much so that it understands when taught and submits when struck—clearly teaching us that he has subjected all things to us, because we have been made according to the image of the Creator (Genesis 1:26). And not only in the large animals is it possible to behold the unsearchable wisdom of God; in the very smallest, no less, we can gather the same wonder. For just as I do not marvel more at the great peaks of the mountains, which by being near the clouds preserve their wintry character through constant exposure to the winds, than at the hollow in the ravines, which not only escapes the harsh winds of the heights but also keeps the air always warm—so also in the construction of animals I do not admire the elephant for its size more than the mouse, because the mouse is feared by the elephant; or the scorpion's very fine sting, how the Craftsman hollowed it out like a pipe, so that through it the venom is injected into those who are struck. And let no one accuse the Maker on this account, that he has introduced venomous and destructive creatures that are hostile to our life. Otherwise one might as well accuse a tutor who brings the easy-going ways of youth into order and disciplines what is undisciplined with blows and whips.
orientation: Basil is still describing how God fitted each land animal's body to its food and life, and now turns to the bear, lion, tiger, and especially the elephant, before drawing a lesson about God's wisdom in both great and small creatures.

title: The plural 'Let us make man' silences Jewish objections
english: The wild beasts are a demonstration of faith. Have you trusted in the Lord? Upon asp and basilisk you will tread, and you will trample lion and dragon (Psalm 90:13 (LXX; Hebrew 91:13)). And you have through faith the authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions (Luke 10:19). Or do you not see that when Paul was gathering sticks, the viper fastened on him and caused him no harm, because the holy man was found to be full of faith (Acts 28:3-5)? But if you are faithless, fear not so much the wild beast as your own faithlessness, through which you have made yourself easy prey to every corruption.

But indeed I sense that I have long been called upon to speak about the creation of man, and I almost seem to hear my hearers crying out in their hearts, 'We are being taught what sort of nature our own things have, but we are ignorant of ourselves.' So I must speak, having pushed aside the hesitation that holds us. For truly it seems to be the most difficult thing of all to know oneself. Not only does the eye, which sees things outside, not use its seeing upon itself, but also our very mind, which sharply discerns another's sin, is slow to recognize its own defects. For this reason even now my discourse, having swiftly gone through things outside us, is sluggish and full of hesitation when it comes to examining our own affairs. And yet it is no more possible to know God from heaven and earth than from our own constitution, at least for the one who examines himself intelligently. As the prophet says, 'Your knowledge became wonderful from me' (Psalm 138:6 (LXX; Hebrew 139:6))—that is, by learning to know myself, I was taught the surpassing greatness of the wisdom in you.

And God said, 'Let us make man' (Genesis 1:26). Where now is the Jew who, in the passages before, when the light of theology was shining through as if through certain windows, and a second Person was being indicated mystically but not yet clearly revealed, fought against the truth, saying that God was conversing with himself? For he himself said, he says, and he himself made. 'Let there be light,' and there was light (Genesis 1:3). Even then, of course, the absurdity in what they said was obvious. For what blacksmith, or carpenter, or leatherworker, sitting alone with the tools of his trade and with no one working with him, says to himself, 'Let us make the knife,' or 'Let us fit together the plow,' or 'Let us finish the sandal'? Does he not rather carry out the work before him in silence? For it is truly terrible nonsense to say that someone sits as ruler and overseer of himself, giving orders to himself in a lordly and urgent manner. But still, those who did not hesitate to slander the Lord himself—what would they not say, having tongues trained for falsehood? The present word, however, completely stops their mouth. 'And God said, Let us make man.' Tell me, is the Person solitary even now? For it is not written, 'Let man be made,' but 'Let us make man.' As long as the one being taught had not yet appeared, the proclamation of theology was hidden in depth. But when the creation of man is now expected, the faith is laid bare, and the doctrine of the truth is shown more clearly. 'Let us make man.' Do you hear, O fighter against Christ, that he is conversing with the partner of his creation, through whom he also made the ages, who upholds all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:2-3)? But he does not quietly accept the word of piety. Just as the most man-hating of wild beasts, when they are shut up in cages, roar around the bars, showing the bitter and savage character of their nature but unable to fulfill their rage, so also the race hostile to the truth, the Jews, being hard pressed, say, 'There are many persons to whom the word of God was addressed.'
orientation: Basil is concluding his treatment of the land animals and turning to the creation of humanity, where he will argue that the plural verb in Genesis 1:26 reveals the Father speaking to the Son.

title: Against Jewish and Anomoian denials of the Son's co-creative dignity
english: For they say he is speaking to the angels who stand beside him: 'Let us make man.' The fabrication is Jewish, the myth-making born of their ease in argument. So that they may not accept the one, they introduce countless persons. And rejecting the Son, they attach the dignity of counsel to servants, and make our fellow slaves lords of our creation. A man who is being perfected is raised up to the dignity of angels. But what created thing can be equal to its creator? Consider also what follows: 'According to our image.' What do you say to this? Is there one image of God and of angels? For of the Son and the Father there is every necessity that the form be the same—the form being understood, of course, in a way befitting God, not in bodily shape, but in the distinctive character of the Godhead. Hear also, you who are from the new mutilation, you who promote Judaism under the pretense of Christianity. To whom does he say, 'According to our image'? To whom else but the radiance of his glory and the exact impress of his substance, who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15)? To his own living image, then, to the one who said, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), and 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9)—to this one he says, 'Let us make man according to our image' (Genesis 1:26). Where there is one image, where is the dissimilarity? 'And God made the man' (Genesis 1:27). He did not say, 'They made.' Here he fled from the plurality of persons. Through those words he instructs the Jew, and through these he shuts out Hellenism, and he safely ran back up to the monad, so that you may understand the Son with the Father, and may escape the danger of polytheism. 'In the image of God he made him' (Genesis 1:27). Again he introduced the person of the co-worker. For he did not say, 'In his own image,' but, 'In the image of God.' In what respect, then, man has that which is according to the image of God, and how he receives a share of that which is according to the likeness, will be said in what follows, God granting it. But for now let this much be said: if there is one image, where did you get the idea to commit unbearable impiety, saying that the Son is unlike the Father? O the ingratitude! The likeness you received, this you do not share with your benefactor? And you think that the things granted to you by grace remain yours by right, but you do not permit the Son to have the likeness to the one who begot him that is his by nature? But the evening now commands us to silence, having long ago sent the sun toward its setting. Here, then, let us also put the word to rest, content with what has been said. For now we have touched upon the matter only enough to awaken your zeal for the word; but we will give a more complete examination of the things before us in what follows, with the cooperation of the Spirit. Go in joy, O Christ-loving church, adorning your august tables with the memory of what has been said instead of every costly dish and varied seasoning. Let the one who says the Son is unlike be put to shame; let the Jew be confounded; let the pious rejoice in the doctrines of the truth; let the Lord be glorified, to whom be glory and might forever and ever. Amen.
orientation: Basil is closing his exposition of Genesis 1:26, refuting the Jewish evasion that God addressed angels, and the Anomoian denial that the Son shares the Father's image.
